GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA: A Near-optimal Algorithm for Low-precision Quantization with Low-rank Adaptation

Shihao Zhang Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of California San Diego
shz051@ucsd.edu    Rayan Saab Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Halıcıoğlu Data Science Institute, University of California San Diego
rsaab@ucsd.edu
Abstract

Post-training quantization is widely used for compressing large neural networks, but aggressive low-bit quantization can significantly degrade model quality. A common remedy is to augment the quantized weights with a low-rank correction, leading to approximations of the form W≈Q+L​RW\approx Q+LR. In this paper, we study this low-precision plus low-rank representation through the layer-wise reconstruction objective ‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2}, where XX is a calibration matrix. We establish, to our knowledge, the first information-theoretic lower bounds for this problem under finite-alphabet and bounded low-rank compensation constraints. We then propose GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA, a training-free algorithm that incorporates the low-rank correction directly into a GPTQ-style (Frantar et al. [23]) quantization pass by appropriately augmenting the calibration Hessian. For the choice L=VrL=V_{r}, where VrV_{r} contains the top right singular vectors of XX, we prove layer-wise reconstruction error bounds in which the usual GPTQ dependence on ‖X‖F2\|X\|_{F}^{2} is replaced by the rank-rr residual ‖X−Xr‖F2\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}, up to regularization terms. Under natural structural assumptions, these bounds match the information-theoretic lower bounds in their dominant scaling, up to constants and mild factors. We also introduce Bid-Up, a fixed-grid quantization refinement step that can be alternated with optimal low-rank compensation with guaranteed non-increasing layer-wise reconstruction error. Experiments on Qwen3 language models and DeiT vision transformers show that GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA improves over GPTQ and GPTQ followed by low-rank compensation, with additional gains from refinement loops.

1 Introduction

Large neural networks, including transformer based large language models (LLMs) are revolutionizing a wide range of applications like natural language processing, content generation, robotics as well as vision and reasoning tasks. However, such models require substantial memory to store their weights and considerable computational resources for inference. Consequently, the demand for post training model size reduction and inference optimization has grown [52, 15, 10], especially in the need of deploying LLMs on resource-constrained devices. Common approaches for compressing deep neural networks include low-rank approximation [88, 8, 85], pruning [11, 30, 22] and quantization [25, 43, 67].

When used alone, low-precision quantization has been established as a mainstream compression technique for its superior performance [37, 73]. By reducing the number of bits used to represent weights (and activations), quantization lowers storage requirements, memory bandwidth, and computation costs. Post-training quantization (PTQ) [48, 23, 82, 86] is a particularly attractive approach because of its simplicity. It avoids backpropagation and adapts pre-trained models usually in a single pass or in very few passes over a small calibration data set. However, pushing PTQ into sub-4-bit regimes with minimal model degradation is still challenging due to limited representation capacity. Thus, a combination of the three compression techniques mentioned above becomes a natural remedy. At a high level, this leads to a matrix decomposition viewpoint, in which neural network weight matrices are approximated by structured representations that incorporate low-precision, low-rank, or sparse components. More specifically, given a weight matrix WW, one seeks an approximation W~\widetilde{W} of one of the forms W~=L​R+S\widetilde{W}=LR+S, W~=Q+S\widetilde{W}=Q+S, or W~=Q+L​R\widetilde{W}=Q+LR, corresponding respectively to low-rank plus sparse, low-precision plus sparse, and low-precision plus low-rank decompositions.

Low-rank plus sparse matrix decomposition is the basis of robust principal component analysis [5]. It has been rigorously studied in the context of compressed sensing [90, 60] and discrete optimization [3], and it has been applied to the compression of deep neural networks [76, 84, 83]. Similarly, the combination of low-precision quantization and sparsity has also been used for compressing LLMs [17, 36].

In this paper, we focus on the third approach, namely low-precision plus low-rank decomposition. In practice, this often arises by applying low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [31] to a quantized model [18]. Specifically, LoRA fine-tuning keeps the matrix of “base” weights fixed, and adaptation is achieved by learning a low-rank update L​RLR that is added to it. In our setting, the base weights are quantized. This parameterization greatly reduces the number of trainable parameters. This Q+L​RQ+LR approach has been empirically shown to recover much of the expressive power of the original full-precision pretrained model, as we will see when we review the relevant literature in Section 2. Nevertheless, despite substantial work on algorithmic and systems aspects of combining low-precision quantization with low-rank adaptation, a theoretical treatment remains lacking. The empirical observation that a LoRA-finetuned quantized model can achieve performance close to that of its full-precision counterpart naturally leads to two central questions:

How well can a matrix be approximated by the sum of a low-rank matrix and a low-precision matrix, and can such an approximation be computed efficiently?

The first question concerns information-theoretic lower bounds, while the second concerns the design of efficient and scalable algorithms with guarantees on the approximation error. In this paper, we answer both questions affirmatively.

Notation. Throughout the paper, the weight matrix of a layer is denoted by W∈ℝN×N′W\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}, where each of the N′N^{\prime} columns represents a NN-dimensional channel. 𝒜\mathcal{A} denotes the discrete quantization grid (or alphabet) used for weight quantization. In a low-precision plus low-rank decomposition, Q∈𝒜N×N′Q\in\mathcal{A}^{N\times N^{\prime}} will be reserved for the low-precision component and L∈ℝN×r,R∈ℝr×N′L\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times r},\,R\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times N^{\prime}} for the left and right low-rank factors.

For a grid 𝒜\mathcal{A}, we associate a memoryless scalar quantizer (MSQ) 𝒬:ℝ→𝒜\mathcal{Q}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathcal{A} given by 𝒬⁡(z):=arg⁡minp∈𝒜​|z−p|,\mathcal{Q}(z):=\arg\min_{p\in\mathcal{A}}|z-p|, which essentially executes a “round to nearest” (RTN) operation. Given a vector v∈ℝnv\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we use viv_{i} for its ii-th entry, v≥jv_{\geq j} for the subvector (vj,…,vn)⊤(v_{j},\dots,v_{n})^{\top}, and we define v≤jv_{\leq j} analogously. ‖v‖\|v\| is the Euclidean norm of vv. Given a matrix A∈ℝm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, we use AiA_{i} to denote its ii-th column. We use A≥jA_{\geq j} to denote the submatrix (Aj,…,An)(A_{j},\dots,A_{n}). We use col​(A)\text{col}(A) to denote the column space of AA. PAP_{A} is the orthogonal projection onto col​(A)\text{col}(A), and PA⟂P_{A^{\perp}} the projection onto its orthogonal complement. The ∥⋅∥∞\|\cdot\|_{\infty} norm on a matrix refers to the entry-wise infinity norm. Throughout this paper, all indices start from 1, following the standard mathematical convention.

In the experimental section of this paper, we focus on asymmetric per-channel PTQ. Let {0,1,…,2b−1}\{0,1,\dots,2^{b}\!-\!1\} represent the bb-bit uniform integer grid. The standard asymmetric weight quantizer uses its scaled and shifted version 𝒜={s⋅(k−z):k=0,…,2b−1},\mathcal{A}=\{s\cdot(k-z):k=0,\dots,2^{b}\!-\!1\}, where ss is the scaling factor and zz is the offset (zero point) defined per channel (column) w∈ℝNw\in\mathbb{R}^{N} of WW. In asymmetric quantization, ss is typically defined on a scaled min–max grid by s=β⁡(max⁡(w)−min⁡(w))2b−1,s=\frac{\beta(\max(w)-\min(w))}{2^{b}-1}, and we follow the standard choice of zero point z=⌈−min⁡(w)max⁡(w)−min⁡(w)⋅(2b−1)⌋z=\left\lceil\frac{-\min(w)}{\max(w)-\min(w)}\cdot(2^{b}-1)\right\rfloor. The associated RTN operator 𝒬\mathcal{Q} in this case is

𝒬⁡(⋆)=s⋅(clip​(⌈⋆s+z⌋,0,2b−1)−z),\mathcal{Q}(\star)=s\cdot\left(\text{clip}\!\left(\left\lceil\tfrac{\star}{s}+z\right\rfloor;0,2^{b}-1\right)-z\right),

where clip​(x,amin,amax)=min⁡{max⁡{x,amin},amax}\text{clip}(x;a_{\min},a_{\max})=\min\{\max\{x,a_{\min}\},a_{\max}\}.

Layer-wise reconstruction. When compressing a layer WW into W~\widetilde{W}, the goal is to preserve the input–output behavior of the neural network. Consequently, it is not necessary that W~\widetilde{W} be close to WW in a matrix norm. On the other hand, optimizing W~\widetilde{W} with respect to the end-to-end training loss typically requires additional retraining of the model, which can be prohibitively expensive for large-scale neural networks. An alternative is to perform block-wise reconstruction, where multiple layers are optimized jointly to match intermediate activations [32, 40]. However, such approaches often scale poorly with the size of modern large language models due to the resulting dimensionality of the optimization problem. As a result, many post-training compression methods rely on layer-wise reconstruction, where each layer is compressed sequentially, one at a time, by minimizing the discrepancy between the outputs of the original and compressed layer while keeping the rest of the network fixed. The post training quantization algorithm GPTQ [23], which we will mention briefly in Section 2 and introduce with more details in Section 4.1, falls into this regime. This layer-wise approach leads to substantially more manageable optimization problems and enables efficient training-free compression of very large models [23, 22, 8, 77]. Throughout this paper, we will use X∈ℝm×NX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N} to denote the input calibration dataset of mm samples (e.g., tokens) stored in rows, resulting in the loss function ‖X​W−X​W~‖F2\|XW-X\widetilde{W}\|_{F}^{2}.

Thus, in the case of W~=Q+L​R\widetilde{W}=Q+LR, the optimization problem becomes

minimizeQ∈𝒜N×N′,L∈ℝN×r,R∈ℝr×N′​‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2.\underset{Q\in\mathcal{A}^{N\times N^{\prime}},L\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times r},R\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times N^{\prime}}}{\mathrm{minimize}}\ \|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2}. (1)

Here we slightly abuse our notation by using the same symbol 𝒜\mathcal{A} for all columns (or blocks of entries within columns), when each column (or block) may have its own grid (i.e. zero point and scaling constant).

1.1 Contributions and Roadmap

We began by formulating the layer-wise low-precision plus low-rank compression problem as the reconstruction objective (1), where a weight matrix WW is approximated by Q+L​RQ+LR. With that formulation in hand, our main contributions are as follows.

  • •

    Information-theoretic lower bounds. We prove information-theoretic lower bounds for approximation by low-precision plus low-rank representations. We first show in Theorem 3.1 that an unconstrained integer alphabet together with a rank-one correction is already dense, which explains why finite-alphabet and bounded-magnitude assumptions are necessary for meaningful lower bounds. Under these constraints, Theorem 3.5 gives a worst-case lower bound for general matrices, Corollary 3.8 extends the bound to a non-spiky class of matrices, and Corollary 3.9 converts this into a lower bound for the layer-wise reconstruction error.

  • •

    GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA. After reviewing GPTQ [23] in Section 4.1, we introduce GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA, a training-free algorithm that incorporates the low-rank correction directly into a GPTQ-style quantization pass. The method chooses the left factor L=VrL=V_{r}, where VrV_{r} contains the top right singular vectors of the calibration matrix XX, and then runs GPTQ on an augmented Hessian to produce both the low-precision component QQ and the error absorption factor RR. The construction is described in Sections 4.2 and 3.

  • •

    Upper bounds on the error. We prove layer-wise reconstruction error bounds for GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA. The channel-wise bound in Theorem 4.3, its unregularized least squares analogue in Theorem 4.5, and the layer-wise bounds in Corollaries 4.6 and 4.7 show that the usual GPTQ dependence on ‖X‖F2\|X\|_{F}^{2} can be replaced by the rank-rr residual ‖X−Xr‖F2\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}, up to the regularization contribution. We also discuss in Remark 4.9 how these infinite-alphabet estimates should be interpreted under a finite quantization alphabet.

  • •

    Near optimality of GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA. We compare the lower and upper bounds in Section 4.4. Under an approximate rank-rr structure for the calibration matrix and a non-spikiness assumption on WW, the upper bound for GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA matches the information-theoretic lower bound in its dominant dependence on the alphabet size and on the smallest singular value of XX, up to constants and mild factors.

  • •

    Bid-Up. We propose Bid-Up, a fixed-grid coordinate refinement step for the quantized component QQ, and combine it with the Optimal Low-rank Compensation (OLrC) technique from Algorithm 1 to refine both the low-precision and low-rank components. Each OLrC step optimizes the low-rank compensation for fixed QQ, while each Bid-Up coordinate update exactly minimizes over the fixed quantization grid, so a full refinement loop cannot increase the layer-wise reconstruction error, but may decrease it. The method is described in Sections 5 and 4.

  • •

    Numerical Validation. We validate the method empirically on language models and vision transformers. The Qwen3 experiments in Table 1 show that GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA improves over GPTQ and over GPTQ followed by OLrC, especially in low-bit regimes. The DeiT-B and DeiT-III-L experiments in Tables 2 and 3 show analogous gains for vision transformers, as well as further improvements from additional OLrC and Bid-Up refinement loops.

2 Related Work

To the best of our knowledge, there has been very limited theoretical investigation of the optimization problem (1), and of error bounds associated with methods that approximate its solution. In contrast, a substantial body of empirical and algorithmic work has been developed. Important works applying LoRA style finetuning to quantization include QLoRA [18] and QA-LoRA[71]. They follow the original LoRA’s[31] “Noise & Zeros” initialization scheme with a focus on reducing memory usage during finetuning and improving inference efficiency. LoftQ [41] and LQ-LoRA [26] initialize the low-rank factors LL and RR so that L​RLR is the best low-rank approximation of W−QW\!-\!Q given by singular value decomposition (SVD, by e.g. Eckart-Young theorem[19]) and finetune the low-rank factors from that. The idea of using the SVD to shrink the gap between QQ and WW was introduced earlier in [74] as Low Rank Compensation (LoRC). SVDQuant [39] explores a similar approach in a different order, where one first computes an SVD to find a low-rank approximation L​RLR for WW and then quantizes the remainder W−L​RW-LR to obtain QQ.

Calibrated LoRA Initialization. Going beyond initializations that are independent of calibration data, LQER [78] leverages an activation induced scale matrix to initialize the low-rank factors. To further enhance initialization, more recent works such as QERA [79], CALDERA [55], EoRA [45] and CLoQ [16] have all converged to an approach involving approximately solving the layer-wise reconstruction problem (1). A common theme in these four methods is that the quantized matrix QQ is fixed first, after which the low-rank factors are obtained by solving the rank-constrained reconstruction problem

minimizeL∈ℝN×r,R∈ℝr×N′​‖X⁡(W−Q)−X​L​R‖F2,\underset{L\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times r},R\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times N^{\prime}}}{\mathrm{minimize}}\ \|X(W-Q)-XLR\|_{F}^{2}, (2)

for a prescribed rank rr and calibration matrix XX.

In particular, [55, 45, 16] obtain QQ via the GPTQ[23] or LDLQ[6] algorithms (which are known to be equivalent). The rank constrained regression problem (2) admits an explicit solution via the generalized singular value decomposition (GSVD) [57]. The use of GSVD for low-rank approximation in neural networks appears at least as early as [88]. Assuming that X⊤​XX^{\top}X is invertible, an optimal product is given by

L⋆​R⋆=(X⊤​X)−12​𝒯r​((X⊤​X)12​(W−Q)),L^{\star}R^{\star}=(X^{\top}X)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{T}_{r}\big((X^{\top}X)^{\frac{1}{2}}(W-Q)\big), (3)

where 𝒯r\mathcal{T}_{r} returns a best rank-rr approximation, computed by truncated SVD. We summarize this solution to (2) in Algorithm 1 and present more background on the GSVD in Appendix B. Consequently, the minimum value in (2) is characterized by the following proposition.

Proposition 2.1.

Let M∈ℝN×N′M\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}} and X∈ℝm×NX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N}, and assume that H=X⊤​XH=X^{\top}X is invertible. Then

minL∈ℝN×r,R∈ℝr×N′​‖X​M−X​L​R‖F2=‖H12​M−𝒯r​(H12​M)‖F2.\underset{L\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times r},R\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times N^{\prime}}}{\min}\|XM-XLR\|_{F}^{2}=\|H^{\frac{1}{2}}M-\mathcal{T}_{r}(H^{\frac{1}{2}}M)\|_{F}^{2}.

This closed-form characterization is a common mathematical core underlying these methods. Indeed, the equivalence between the low-rank factors derived in QERA (Theorem 1 in [79]) and CALDERA (Lemma 4.2 in [55]) has already been discussed in Zhang et al. [79, Appendix A.3].11 1 One caveat is that CALDERA allows the low-rank factors LL and RR to be generated directly in low precision. One can similarly verify that CLoQ (Theorem 3.1 in [16]) and EoRA (Theorem 1 in [45]) lead to the same mathematical formulation.

ApiQ [44] targets a modified version of (1) that uses two calibration matrices, one sampled from the full-precision model and one sampled from the quantized model. It uses a back-propagation-based procedure to minimize the layer-wise, or block-wise, reconstruction error by jointly training the low-rank factors L,RL,R and the quantization parameters for QQ. As a result, ApiQ is more computationally expensive than the closed-form initialization methods discussed above and does not provide comparable theoretical guarantees. As a final example, SRR [12] instead splits the rank budget rr into two parts and computes low-rank factors both before and after quantization.

3 Information Theoretic Lower Bounds

In this section, we study the smallest possible value of

‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2}

over all choices of the low-precision component QQ and the low-rank correction L​RLR, regardless of the algorithm used to construct them. To obtain such lower bounds, we first study the simpler approximation error ‖W−(Q+L​R)‖F,\|W-(Q+LR)\|_{F}, and then derive corresponding bounds for ‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2} as corollaries.

We begin with a warm-up result that may initially appear counterintuitive. Any real-valued matrix can be approximated arbitrarily well by the sum of a rank-one matrix and an integer-valued matrix, as the theorem below shows.

Theorem 3.1.

Let W∈ℝN×N′W\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}} be any matrix, and let δ>0\delta>0. Then, for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exist Z∈ℤN×N′Z\in\mathbb{Z}^{N\times N^{\prime}}, a∈ℝNa\in\mathbb{R}^{N}, and b∈ℝN′b\in\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}} such that

‖W−(δ​Z+a​b⊤)‖op<ϵ.\|W-(\delta Z+ab^{\top})\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\epsilon.

Equivalently, the set

𝕊δ1:={δZ+Λ:Z∈ℤN×N′,Λ∈ℝN×N′,rank(Λ)≤1}\mathbb{S}_{\delta}^{1}:=\{\delta Z+\Lambda:Z\in\mathbb{Z}^{N\times N^{\prime}},\,\Lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}},\,\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\leq}1\}

is dense in ℝN×N′\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}.

The proof is deferred to Appendix A. The following corollary is immediate.

Corollary 3.2.

For any X∈ℝm×NX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N} and δ>0\delta>0, the set

{X(δQ+Λ):Q∈ℤN×N′,Λ∈ℝN×N′,rank(Λ)≤1}\{X(\delta Q+\Lambda):Q\in\mathbb{Z}^{N\times N^{\prime}},\,\Lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}},\,\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\leq}1\}

is dense in {X​W:W∈ℝN×N′}.\{XW:W\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}\}.

Since the set 𝕊δ1,\mathbb{S}_{\delta}^{1}, defined in Theorem 3.1, is dense in ℝN×N′\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}, it follows immediately that for any r≥1r\geq 1 the larger set 𝕊δ≤r={δQ+Λ:Q∈ℤN×N′,Λ∈ℝN×N′,rank(Λ)≤r}\mathbb{S}_{\delta}^{\leq r}=\{\delta Q+\Lambda:Q\in\mathbb{Z}^{N\times N^{\prime}},\,\Lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}},\,\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda)\leq r\} is also dense in ℝN×N′\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}.

This observation is mathematically striking and it suggests that even a rank-one correction can absorb all the quantization error, but it does not reflect what one observes in practice. In practice, a rank-one correction is not sufficient to recover the performance of a heavily quantized model, and increasing the rank does lead to meaningful empirical improvements. The reason is that the density result exploits the unboundedness of ℤN×N′\mathbb{Z}^{N\times N^{\prime}}. In practical compression, the quantized component QQ must be represented using a finite number of bits, and the entries of the low-rank correction Λ\Lambda cannot be arbitrarily large. Thus, a more realistic model should constrain the number of values available to each entry of QQ, while still allowing the grid spacing δ\delta to adapt to the scale of WW. It should also impose a magnitude constraint on the low-rank component. This motivates the following definition.

Definition 3.3.

For positive integers rr and BB, and a positive real number ρ\rho, define the constrained low-precision plus low-rank class by

𝕊Br,ρ:={δQ+Λ:δ>0,Q∈ℤN×N′,∥Q∥∞≤B,Λ∈ℝN×N′,rank(Λ)≤r,∥Λ∥F≤ρ}.\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho}:=\left\{\delta Q+\Lambda:\delta>0,\ Q\in\mathbb{Z}^{N\times N^{\prime}},\ \|Q\|_{\infty}\leq B,\ \Lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}},\ \operatorname{rank}(\Lambda)\leq r,\ \|\Lambda\|_{F}\leq\rho\right\}.

Here ‖Q‖∞\|Q\|_{\infty} denotes the entrywise infinity norm, so QQ uses a scaled alphabet of size 2​B+12B+1, while ρ\rho controls the size of the low-rank correction.

With this definition, the quantized component QQ is restricted to a finite alphabet, while the grid spacing δ>0\delta>0 remains free to adapt to the scale of the matrix being approximated. The low-rank component Λ\Lambda is also required to have bounded Frobenius norm. To normalize the problem, we restrict our attention to matrices in the unit Frobenius ball 𝔹F1:={A∈ℝN×N′:‖A‖F≤1}\mathbb{B}_{F}^{1}:=\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}:\|A\|_{F}\leq 1\}. The question is whether the constrained class 𝕊Br,ρ\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho} can still be dense in this unit ball. Suppose A∈𝔹F1A\in\mathbb{B}_{F}^{1}, ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), and M∈𝕊Br,ρM\in\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho} satisfies ‖M−A‖F≤ϵ\|M-A\|_{F}\leq\epsilon. Then, by the triangle inequality, ‖M‖F≤‖A‖F+ϵ<2\|M\|_{F}\leq\|A\|_{F}+\epsilon<2. Thus, when studying ϵ\epsilon-approximations to matrices in 𝔹F1\mathbb{B}_{F}^{1}, it suffices to consider elements in 𝕊Br,ρ∩𝔹F2\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho}\cap\mathbb{B}_{F}^{2}.

We need the following auxiliary lemma on the covering number of low-rank matrices with bounded Frobenius norm. Its proof, which is standard, can be found in Appendix A.

Lemma 3.4.

Let 𝕊r,ρ:={Λ∈ℝN×N′:rank(Λ)≤r,∥Λ∥F≤ρ}.\mathbb{S}^{r,\rho}:=\{\Lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}:\operatorname{rank}(\Lambda)\leq r,\ \|\Lambda\|_{F}\leq\rho\}. Then, for 0<ϵ≤ρ0<\epsilon\leq\rho, its covering number in the Frobenius metric satisfies

𝒩(ϵ,∥⋅∥F,𝕊r,ρ)≤(10​ρϵ)r⁡(N+N′+1)+1.\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\|\cdot\|_{F},\mathbb{S}^{r,\rho})\leq\left(\frac{10\rho}{\epsilon}\right)^{r(N+N^{\prime}+1)+1}.

Now we state and prove the main result of this section.

Theorem 3.5 (Information-theoretic Lower Bound on Approximating General Matrices).

Assume that r⁡(N+N′+1)+2<N​N′r(N+N^{\prime}+1)+2<NN^{\prime}, N​N′>28NN^{\prime}>28 and ρ>19\rho>\frac{1}{9}. Then

supA∈𝔹F1infM∈𝕊Br,ρ∩𝔹F2​‖M−A‖F≥2041⋅1(2​B+1)JJ−1​(41​ρ)1J−1,\underset{A\in\mathbb{B}_{F}^{1}}{\sup}\quad\underset{M\in\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho}\cap\mathbb{B}_{F}^{2}}{\inf}\|M-A\|_{F}\geq\frac{20}{41}\cdot\dfrac{1}{(2B+1)^{\frac{J}{J-1}}(41\rho)^{\frac{1}{J-1}}},

where

J=J⁡(r,N,N′)=N​N′r⁡(N+N′+1)+2∈(1,+∞).J=J(r,N,N^{\prime})=\frac{NN^{\prime}}{r(N+N^{\prime}+1)+2}\in(1,+\infty).

Before proving the theorem, we provide a brief interpretation of the lower bound.

Remark 3.6.

The parameter JJ measures how small the allowed low rank component is relative to the ambient dimension. Indeed, larger JJ corresponds to a smaller rank budget relative to the size of the matrix. Under the assumptions of the theorem, the right side of the bound increases with JJ. Thus, as the allowed low rank component becomes more restrictive, the worst case approximation error necessarily becomes larger.

Recall also that 2​B+12B+1 is the size of the integer alphabet {−B,…,−1,0,1,…,B}\{-B,\ldots,-1,0,1,\ldots,B\} used for each entry of QQ, up to the scaling factor δ\delta. The theorem shows that the lower bound scales as ρ−1/(J−1)\rho^{-1/(J-1)} in the magnitude budget for the low rank component, and as (2B+1)−J/(J−1)(2B+1)^{-J/(J-1)} in the alphabet size. Thus, increasing either the allowed low rank magnitude or the quantization alphabet improves the best possible approximation, but with rates controlled by the effective compression parameter JJ.

Now we prove Theorem 3.5.

Remark 3.7.

The same lower bound remains valid even if the supremum over 𝔹F1\mathbb{B}_{F}^{1} is restricted to a class of non-spiky matrices. More precisely, for an absolute constant CC, the same bound holds with 𝔹F1\mathbb{B}_{F}^{1} replaced by

𝔹F1∩{A∈ℝN×N′:‖A‖∞≤C​log⁡(N​N′)N​N′}.\mathbb{B}_{F}^{1}\cap\left\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}:\|A\|_{\infty}\leq C\frac{\log(NN^{\prime})}{\sqrt{NN^{\prime}}}\right\}.

Indeed, let d=N​N′d=NN^{\prime}. After vectorizing matrices in ℝN×N′\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}} as vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and rescaling by d\sqrt{d}, we obtain

Vol⁡(𝔹F1∩{A∈ℝN×N′:‖A‖∞≤C​log⁡(N​N′)N​N′})Vol⁡(𝔹F1)=ℙx∼Unif⁡(𝔹⁡(0,d))(∥x∥∞≤Clogd).\frac{\operatorname{Vol}\left(\mathbb{B}_{F}^{1}\cap\left\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}:\|A\|_{\infty}\leq C\frac{\log(NN^{\prime})}{\sqrt{NN^{\prime}}}\right\}\right)}{\operatorname{Vol}(\mathbb{B}_{F}^{1})}=\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathbb{B}(0,\sqrt{d}))}\left(\|x\|_{\infty}\leq C\log d\right).

The uniform distribution on the Euclidean ball 𝔹⁡(0,d)⊂ℝd\mathbb{B}(0,\sqrt{d})\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is subgaussian [65]. Therefore, by choosing CC sufficiently large, the probability on the right is at least 1−1/d1-1/d, and hence at least 3/43/4 when N,N′≥2N,N^{\prime}\geq 2. Since the proof above shows that Vol⁡(Uϵ)<12​Vol⁡(𝔹F1)\operatorname{Vol}(U_{\epsilon})<\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Vol}(\mathbb{B}_{F}^{1}), it follows that

Vol⁡(Uϵ)<23​Vol⁡(𝔹F1∩{A∈ℝN×N′:‖A‖∞≤C​log⁡(N​N′)N​N′}).\operatorname{Vol}(U_{\epsilon})<\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{Vol}\left(\mathbb{B}_{F}^{1}\cap\left\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}:\|A\|_{\infty}\leq C\frac{\log(NN^{\prime})}{\sqrt{NN^{\prime}}}\right\}\right).

Thus this restricted class still contains a matrix at distance larger than ϵ\epsilon from 𝕊Br,ρ∩𝔹F2\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho}\cap\mathbb{B}_{F}^{2}, and the same lower bound holds. In other words, 𝕊Br,ρ\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho} is not dense even in a non-spiky subset of the unit Frobenius ball. Non-spiky matrices are especially relevant in post training quantization. A recent line of work applies preprocessing transformations that exploit invariances in the computation graph, often of the form X​W=(X​T−1)​(T​W)XW=(XT^{-1})(TW). The most common examples are rotations, where T−1=T⊤T^{-1}=T^{\top}, including Hadamard rotations [1], random rotations [6], and learned rotations [47]. These transformations are designed to reduce the dynamic range of WW, thereby promoting flatness, or incoherence, of the transformed weights. Post training compression is then applied to the transformed matrix T​WTW.

With a more refined volume estimate, we can strengthen this observation to an even flatter class of matrices in the following corollary. The proof is deferred to Appendix A.

Corollary 3.8 (Information Theoretic Lower Bound for Non-spiky Matrices).

Let

𝔹flat1:=𝔹F1∩{A∈ℝN×N′:‖A‖∞≤3N​N′}.\mathbb{B}_{\mathrm{flat}}^{1}:=\mathbb{B}_{F}^{1}\cap\left\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}:\|A\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{NN^{\prime}}}\right\}.

Assume that r⁡(N+N′+1)+2<N​N′r(N+N^{\prime}+1)+2<NN^{\prime}, N​N′≥144NN^{\prime}\geq 144, and ρ>19\rho>\frac{1}{9}. Then

supA∈𝔹flat1infM∈𝕊Br,ρ∩𝔹F2‖M−A‖F≥2041⋅1(2​B+1)JJ−1​(41​π​e6​ρ)1J−1,\sup_{A\in\mathbb{B}_{\mathrm{flat}}^{1}}\inf_{M\in\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho}\cap\mathbb{B}_{F}^{2}}\|M-A\|_{F}\geq\frac{20}{41}\cdot\frac{1}{(2B+1)^{\frac{J}{J-1}}\left(41\sqrt{\frac{\pi e}{6}}\rho\right)^{\frac{1}{J-1}}},

where J=J⁡(r,N,N′)=N​N′r⁡(N+N′+1)+2∈(1,∞).J=J(r,N,N^{\prime})=\frac{NN^{\prime}}{r(N+N^{\prime}+1)+2}\in(1,\infty).

As a direct consequence, we obtain the corresponding lower bound for layer-wise reconstruction error.

Let X∈ℝm×NX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N}, with m>Nm>N, and assume that σmin​(X)>0\sigma_{\min}(X)>0. Then there exists A∈ℝN×N′A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}} satisfying ‖A‖F≤1\|A\|_{F}\leq 1 and ‖A‖∞≤3/N​N′\|A\|_{\infty}\leq\sqrt{3}/\sqrt{NN^{\prime}} such that
