4 GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA

Having presented lower bounds associated with solving (1), we now propose and analyze a novel algorithm for solving it, GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA. To that end, we first provide a brief overview of GPTQ in Section 4.1, recalling its development from early pruning methods to its current modern formulation. After that, we formally introduce our method in Section 4.2 and provide upper bounds on its associated layer-wise reconstruction error assuming an infinite alphabet. We also provide, in Section 4.3, a remark on interpreting the bounds under a finite alphabet. Finally, we compare the upper bounds in Section 4.3 with the information-theoretic lower bounds established in Section 3 and demonstrate that GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA is near-optimal.

4.1 An Introduction to GPTQ

From pruning to GPTQ.

As the name suggests, our GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA builds upon GPTQ, a widely used baseline in many recent works on PTQ. GPTQ and related algorithms [21, 22, 23] are developed from an older framework that traces back to the Optimal Brain Damage (OBD, LeCun et al. [38]) and Optimal Brain Surgery (OBS, Hassibi et al. [29]) algorithms, originally designed for network pruning. In OBS, pruning is performed iteratively by solving a small optimization problem at each step. Denoting the “Hessian” by H=X⊤​XH=X^{\top}X and letting δw\delta_{w} represent the update to the weight vector, the OBS pruning step solves

minδw​12​δw⊤​H​δwsubject toep⊤​δw+wp=0,δw|F=0,\underset{\delta_{w}}{\min}\ \frac{1}{2}\delta_{w}^{\top}H\delta_{w}\quad\text{subject to}\quad e_{p}^{\top}\delta_{w}+w_{p}=0,\quad\delta_{w}|_{F}=0,

where epe_{p} is the standard basis vector selecting the pp-th coordinate to prune, and δw|F=0\delta_{w}|_{F}=0 enforces no change to already-fixed coordinates indexed by FF (see [28]). This paradigm was adapted to PTQ in Optimal Brain Quantization (OBQ, Frantar and Alistarh [21]). Similar to OBS, each step of OBQ involves solving

minq∈𝒜{minδw12δw⊤Hδwsubject toep⊤δw+wp=q,δw|F=0},\underset{q\in\mathcal{A}}{\min}\left\{\ \underset{\delta_{w}}{\min}\ \frac{1}{2}\delta_{w}^{\top}H\delta_{w}\ \text{subject to}\ e_{p}^{\top}\delta_{w}+w_{p}=q,\quad\delta_{w}|_{F}=0\ \right\},

where 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the quantization alphabet.

In the pruning case, the constrained quadratic problem admits a closed-form solution via the stationary point of its Lagrangian. In the quantization setting, the inner minimization problem remains convex and can be solved in exactly the same way. What is new in quantization is that one must evaluate the objective over all possible choices of qq in a discrete set 𝒜\mathcal{A} and select the minimizer to solve the outer minimization problem. This leads to a local greedy algorithm that alternates between quantizing a coordinate of ww and updating the remaining unquantized coordinates to compensate for the induced error, until all the coordinates are quantized. This greedy strategy is applied to all the weight vectors (i.e. columns of WW) in a layer in parallel and repeated layer-wise sequentially.

Following OBQ, GPTQ (Algorithm 2, Frantar et al. [23]) leverages state-of-the-art Cholesky kernels to improve efficiency and stability, enabling it to scale to very large LLMs. Specifically, GPTQ uses the lower-triangular Cholesky factor Ψ\Psi in the decomposition H−1=Ψ​ΨTH^{-1}=\Psi\Psi^{T} in place of H−1H^{-1} itself as it gives a computationally equivalent output when the Cholesky decomposition exists. A “dampening” term λ​I\lambda I is added to XT​XX^{T}X when computing the inverse Hessian to mitigate numerical instability22 2 Another implementation detail, called lazy batch updates in [23], involves processing the weights in blocks of size BB to enhance the compute-to-memory-access ratio while preserving the algorithm’s mathematical equivalence to the B=1B=1 case. We always consider B=1B=1 in this paper..

GPTQ notation and error diffusion.

We now fix notation for the GPTQ iterations applied to a single weight vector w=(w1,…,wN)⊤∈ℝNw=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{N})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} using a calibration matrix XX. Since GPTQ processes the columns of WW independently in parallel, it suffices to describe the iteration for one column ww. Recall that the rows of X∈ℝm×NX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N} correspond to calibration samples, such as tokens. We write the feature-wise decomposition of XX as X=(X1⋯XN)X=\begin{pmatrix}X_{1}&\cdots&X_{N}\end{pmatrix}, where Xj∈ℝmX_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} denotes the jj-th feature column.

At each step tt, GPTQ rounds the current weight entry using the scalar quantizer 𝒬:ℝ→𝒜\mathcal{Q}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathcal{A}, setting qt=𝒬⁡(wt(t−1))q_{t}=\mathcal{Q}(w_{t}^{(t-1)}). It then updates the remaining unquantized entries as in line 6 of Algorithm 2. It was shown in Zhang et al. [87] that this update is equivalent to

w≥t+1(t)=arg⁡min(vt+1,…,vN)∈ℝN−t​12​‖(qt−wt(t−1))​Xt+∑j=t+1N(vj−wj(t−1))​Xj‖2.w^{(t)}_{\geq t+1}=\underset{(v_{t+1},\dots,v_{N})\in\mathbb{R}^{N-t}}{\arg\min}\,\frac{1}{2}\left\|(q_{t}-w^{(t-1)}_{t})X_{t}+\sum_{j=t+1}^{N}(v_{j}-w^{(t-1)}_{j})X_{j}\right\|^{2}.

Here (qt−wt(t−1))​Xt(q_{t}-w^{(t-1)}_{t})X_{t} is the error introduced by rounding the tt-th entry. The update from w≥t+1(t−1)w^{(t-1)}_{\geq t+1} to w≥t+1(t)w^{(t)}_{\geq t+1} adjusts the remaining weights to minimize the resulting distortion in ℓ2\ell_{2}, a process referred to as error diffusion in [87]. We denote the full state of the algorithm after step tt by

w(t)=(q≤t,w≥t+1(t))∈𝒜t×ℝN−t,w^{(t)}=(q_{\leq t},w^{(t)}_{\geq t+1})\in\mathcal{A}^{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{N-t},

with initialization w(0)=w∈ℝNw^{(0)}=w\in\mathbb{R}^{N} and final output w(N)=q∈𝒜Nw^{(N)}=q\in\mathcal{A}^{N}. We also define the reconstruction error after step tt by

𝐞t=X​w−X​w(t)=X​w−∑j=1tqj​Xj−∑j=t+1Nwj(t)​Xj.{\bf e}_{t}=Xw-Xw^{(t)}=Xw-\sum_{j=1}^{t}q_{j}X_{j}-\sum_{j=t+1}^{N}w^{(t)}_{j}X_{j}. (4)

Finally, applying GPTQ with regularization parameter λ>0\lambda>0, meaning that λ​I\lambda I is added to the Hessian H=X⊤​XH=X^{\top}X, is equivalent to applying unregularized GPTQ to the appended calibration matrix

Xtall=(Xλ​I).X_{\mathrm{tall}}=\begin{pmatrix}X\\ \sqrt{\lambda}I\end{pmatrix}.

Indeed, X⊤​X+λ​I=Xtall⊤​XtallX^{\top}X+\lambda I=X_{\mathrm{tall}}^{\top}X_{\mathrm{tall}}. In particular, XtallX_{\mathrm{tall}} has full column rank, regardless of whether XX itself is full rank or whether m≥Nm\geq N.

4.2 The GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA Construction

Unlike existing methods that treat low-rank adaptation as a separate step after PTQ [79, 55, 16], our approach incorporates the low-rank correction directly into a GPTQ-style quantization pass. More precisely, for a chosen left factor L∈ℝN×rL\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times r}, we construct Q∈𝒜N×N′Q\in\mathcal{A}^{N\times N^{\prime}} and R∈ℝr×N′R\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times N^{\prime}} jointly, using a completely training-free procedure aimed at reducing the layer-wise reconstruction error ‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2}.

For any fixed LL, define X^=X​L\widehat{X}=XL. Then the objective can be rewritten as

‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2=‖X​W−(X​Q+X^​R)‖F2=‖[XX^]​[W0]−[XX^]​[QR]‖F2.\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2}=\|XW-(XQ+\widehat{X}R)\|_{F}^{2}=\left\|\left[\begin{array}[]{c:c}X\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@add@cssclass&\widehat{X}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}W\\ \hline\cr 0\end{array}\right]-\left[\begin{array}[]{c:c}X\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@add@cssclass&\widehat{X}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}Q\\ \hline\cr R\end{array}\right]\right\|_{F}^{2}.

Thus, once LL is fixed, the low-rank correction can be viewed as adding rr extra full-precision columns to the calibration matrix and rr corresponding full-precision rows to the quantized weight representation. This reformulation is visualized in Figure 1.

Generating RR given LL.

Define the augmented calibration matrix and the augmented weight matrix

𝕏=[XX^]∈ℝm×(N+r) and 𝕎=[W0]∈ℝ(N+r)×N′.\mathbb{X}=\left[\begin{array}[]{c:c}X\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@add@cssclass&\widehat{X}\end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times(N+r)}\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathbb{W}=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}W\\ \hline\cr 0\end{array}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+r)\times N^{\prime}}.

Our method entails applying GPTQ to 𝕎\mathbb{W} using the augmented Hessian ℍ=𝕏⊤​𝕏\mathbb{H}=\mathbb{X}^{\top}\mathbb{X}, together with the usual dampening term. However, we run GPTQ for only NN iterations, so that only the first NN rows of 𝕎\mathbb{W} are quantized. The result is a quantized matrix Q∈𝒜N×N′Q\in\mathcal{A}^{N\times N^{\prime}}, together with a full-precision matrix R∈ℝr×N′R\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times N^{\prime}}. Since RR is initialized at zero and updated throughout the NN GPTQ steps, it absorbs the errors generated while sequentially quantizing WW into QQ. For this reason, we refer to RR as the error absorption factor.

Selecting LL.

It remains to choose the left factor LL. Our choice is motivated by the fact that, in the optimal low-rank compensation procedure of Algorithm 1, the column space of the left low-rank factor is spanned by eigenvectors of X⊤​XX^{\top}X, equivalently by right singular vectors of XX. In addition, LL acts as a dimension reduction map on the features of the calibration matrix XX. It is therefore natural to choose LL using principal component analysis. Specifically, if X=U​Σ​V⊤X=U\Sigma V^{\top} is a singular value decomposition of XX, we set L=Vr∈ℝN×rL=V_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times r}, where VrV_{r} contains the first rr columns of VV. We refer to LL as the feature extraction factor.

With this choice of LL, we obtain QQ and RR by running GPTQ for NN iterations on the augmented matrix [W0]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}W\\ \hline\cr 0\end{array}\right] producing the ‘mixed-precision’ [QR]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}Q\\ \hline\cr R\end{array}\right] as described above. A schematic summary of the method is given in Figure 2

Hessian-only implementation.

In many open-source implementations of PTQ algorithms, the calibration data is only used to generate the Hessian H=X⊤​XH=X^{\top}X (or its regularized version), for example as a sum of outer products of the samples with themselves. The calibration matrix XX itself is not explicitly formed, in order to reduce peak memory usage. Our construction can be implemented in this setting as well. If X=U​Σ​V⊤X=U\Sigma V^{\top} is an SVD of XX, then H=V​Σ2​V⊤H=V\Sigma^{2}V^{\top}, so the choice L=VrL=V_{r} can be obtained directly from the eigen-decomposition of HH. The augmented Hessian can then be formed as

ℍ=[HH​VrVr⊤​HVr⊤​H​Vr],\mathbb{H}=\left[\begin{array}[]{c:c}H\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@add@cssclass&HV_{r}\\ \hline\cr V_{r}^{\top}H\hfil\lx@intercol\vrule\lx@add@cssclass&V_{r}^{\top}HV_{r}\end{array}\right],

without explicitly forming either XX or 𝕏\mathbb{X}. We give pseudo code for GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA in Algorithm 3.

Remark 4.1 (Stable factorization of the augmented Hessian).

Because X^=X​L\widehat{X}=XL, the columns of the augmented calibration matrix 𝕏=[X​X^]\mathbb{X}=[X\ \widehat{X}] are linearly dependent whenever r>0r>0. Consequently, the augmented Hessian ℍ=𝕏⊤​𝕏\mathbb{H}=\mathbb{X}^{\top}\mathbb{X} is singular, even when H=X⊤​XH=X^{\top}X is invertible. Thus, standard GPTQ implementations that compute a Cholesky factor of (ℍ+λ​I)−1(\mathbb{H}+\lambda I)^{-1} may become numerically unstable unless one uses a larger regularization parameter λ\lambda. In Algorithm 3, we instead use a more robust procedure for computing the required lower-triangular factor 𝕃\mathbb{L} such that (ℍ+λ​I)−1=𝕃​𝕃⊤(\mathbb{H}+\lambda I)^{-1}=\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L^{\top}}. Specifically, we use an eigen-decomposition together with a QR decomposition to obtain the factor that would ordinarily be produced by a Cholesky decomposition. This allows us to use smaller values of λ\lambda. Further implementation details are given in Appendix C. We emphasize that as Algorithm 3 uses only eigen-decompositions and QR decompositions, it is therefore both gradient-free and SVD-free, despite using a LoRA-style parameterization.

4.3 Upper Bounds on Layer-wise Reconstruction Error

In this section, we prove upper bounds on the layer-wise reconstruction error ‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2} for the choice L=VrL=V_{r}, together with the matrices QQ and RR produced by Algorithm 3.

The algorithm uses the regularized augmented Hessian ℍ+λ​IN+r=𝕏⊤​𝕏+λ​IN+r\mathbb{H}+\lambda I_{N+r}=\mathbb{X}^{\top}\mathbb{X}+\lambda I_{N+r}. As noted in Section 4.1, this is equivalent to applying the unregularized algorithm to the appended augmented data matrix

𝕏+:=(𝕏λ​IN+r)=(XX^λ​I1λ​I2),\mathbb{X}_{+}:=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{X}\\ \sqrt{\lambda}I_{N+r}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}X&\widehat{X}\\ \sqrt{\lambda}I_{1}&\sqrt{\lambda}I_{2}\end{pmatrix},

since 𝕏+⊤​𝕏+=ℍ+λ​IN+r\mathbb{X}_{+}^{\top}\mathbb{X}_{+}=\mathbb{H}+\lambda I_{N+r}. Here

I1=[IN×N0r×N]∈ℝ(N+r)×N,I2=[0N×rIr×r]∈ℝ(N+r)×r.I_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}I_{N\times N}}\\ 0_{r\times N}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+r)\times N},\qquad I_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0_{N\times r}\\ {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}I_{r\times r}}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+r)\times r}.

We also denote the two column blocks of 𝕏+\mathbb{X}_{+} by

X+:=(Xλ​I1)∈ℝ(m+N+r)×N,X^+:=(X^λ​I2)∈ℝ(m+N+r)×r.X_{+}:=\begin{pmatrix}X\\ \sqrt{\lambda}I_{1}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(m+N+r)\times N},\qquad\widehat{X}_{+}:=\begin{pmatrix}\widehat{X}\\ \sqrt{\lambda}I_{2}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(m+N+r)\times r}.

Since X+⊤​X+=X⊤​X+λ​INX_{+}^{\top}X_{+}=X^{\top}X+\lambda I_{N}, the matrices X⊤​XX^{\top}X and X+⊤​X+X_{+}^{\top}X_{+} have the same eigenvectors. Hence XX and X+X_{+} have the same right singular vectors. In particular, if X=U​Σ​V⊤X=U\Sigma V^{\top} is an SVD of XX, then X+=U+​Σ+​V⊤X_{+}=U_{+}\Sigma_{+}V^{\top}, where Σ+\Sigma_{+} has diagonal entries (σi2+λ)1/2(\sigma_{i}^{2}+\lambda)^{1/2}.

Because λ>0\lambda>0, the matrix 𝕏+\mathbb{X}_{+} has full column rank. We may therefore invoke the following GPTQ error evolution lemma, which is the main ingredient in the reconstruction error bounds below.

Lemma 4.2 (Zhang et al. [80]).

Let X∈ℝm×NX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N} be full rank with m≥Nm\geq N, and let w∈ℝNw\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. Running GPTQ with H=X⊤​XH=X^{\top}X using an infinite alphabet 𝒜=𝒜δ={±k​δ:k∈ℤ}\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}^{\delta}=\{\pm k\delta:k\in\mathbb{Z}\}, the error defined in (4) satisfies

𝐞t\displaystyle{\bf e}_{t} =PX≥t+1⟂​(wt(t−1)−qt)​Xt+𝐞t−1​ and ​𝐞N=∑j=1NPX≥j+1⟂​(wj(j−1)−qj)​Xj.\displaystyle=P_{X_{\geq t+1}^{\perp}}(w^{(t-1)}_{t}-q_{t})X_{t}+{\bf e}_{t-1}\text{\hskip 10.22217ptand \hskip 10.22217pt}{\bf e}_{N}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}P_{X_{\geq j+1}^{\perp}}(w^{(j-1)}_{j}-q_{j})X_{j}. (5)

Moreover, the resulting quantized vector qq satisfies

‖X​𝐰−X​𝐪‖22=∑j=1N|wj(j−1)−qj|2​‖PX≥j+1⟂​Xj‖22.\displaystyle\|X\mathbf{w}-X\mathbf{q}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}|w^{(j-1)}_{j}-q_{j}|^{2}\,\|P_{X_{\geq j+1}^{\perp}}X_{j}\|_{2}^{2}. (6)
Theorem 4.3.

Assume an infinite uniform alphabet 𝒜=𝒜δ={±k​δ:k∈ℤ}\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}^{\delta}=\{\pm k\delta:k\in\mathbb{Z}\} and λ>0\lambda>0. If Algorithm 3 is applied with L=VrL=V_{r}, then, for each column 𝐰\mathbf{w} of WW, the corresponding outputs 𝐪\mathbf{q} and 𝐫\mathbf{r} satisfy

‖X​𝐰−X⁡(𝐪+L​𝐫)‖2+λ​‖𝐰−𝐪‖2+λ​‖𝐫‖2≤δ24​(‖X−Xr‖F2+(N+r)​λ).\|X\mathbf{w}-X(\mathbf{q}+L\mathbf{r})\|^{2}+\lambda\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{q}\|^{2}+\lambda\|\mathbf{r}\|^{2}\leq\frac{\delta^{2}}{4}\left(\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}+(N+r)\lambda\right). (7)

We defer the full proof to Appendix A. To illustrate the main idea, we first prove the limiting, unregularized case, corresponding to λ=0\lambda=0, where the argument is cleaner and the role of the low-rank correction is most transparent.

To do this, we use an equivalent least squares formulation of GPTQ. Indeed, although the regularized augmented Hessian ℍ+λ​I\mathbb{H}+\lambda I is invertible for λ>0\lambda>0, the unregularized augmented Hessian ℍ\mathbb{H} is generally singular. Therefore, one cannot implement the λ=0\lambda=0 version of Algorithm 3 through the usual inverse Hessian or Cholesky based GPTQ updates. The least squares formulation avoids this issue and allows the same error evolution argument to be applied directly to the augmented data matrix 𝕏\mathbb{X}. We recall the relevant least squares formulation below.

Lemma 4.4 (Zhang et al. [87]).

Let X∈ℝm×NX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N} have full column rank, with m≥Nm\geq N, and let w∈ℝNw\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. Then the GPTQ iterations with H=X⊤​XH=X^{\top}X are equivalent to the following least squares updates, with w≥1(0)=ww^{(0)}_{\geq 1}=w:

qt\displaystyle q_{t} =arg⁡minp∈𝒜​12​‖X​w−∑j=1t−1qj​Xj−p​Xt−∑j=t+1Nwj(t−1)​Xj‖2,\displaystyle=\underset{p\in\mathcal{A}}{\arg\min}\frac{1}{2}\left\|Xw-\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}q_{j}X_{j}-pX_{t}-\sum_{j=t+1}^{N}w^{(t-1)}_{j}X_{j}\right\|^{2}, (8)
w≥t+1(t)\displaystyle w^{(t)}_{\geq t+1} =arg⁡min(vt+1,…,vN)∈ℝN−t​12​‖X​w−∑j=1tqj​Xj−∑j=t+1Nvj​Xj‖2.\displaystyle=\underset{(v_{t+1},\dots,v_{N})\in\mathbb{R}^{N-t}}{\arg\min}\frac{1}{2}\left\|Xw-\sum_{j=1}^{t}q_{j}X_{j}-\sum_{j=t+1}^{N}v_{j}X_{j}\right\|^{2}. (9)

Moreover, these least squares updates are well defined even when XX is rank deficient or m<Nm<N, although the minimizer in the second update may not be unique. In that case, one may still implement unregularized GPTQ through (9), and the error evolution identity in Lemma 4.2 continues to hold for this formulation.

We now apply this least squares formulation to the augmented matrix 𝕏=[X​X^]\mathbb{X}=[X\ \widehat{X}]. This gives the λ=0\lambda=0 analogue of Theorem 4.3.

Theorem 4.5.

Assume an infinite alphabet 𝒜=𝒜δ={±k​δ:k∈ℤ}\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}^{\delta}=\{\pm k\delta:k\in\mathbb{Z}\}. Consider the unregularized version of Algorithm 3 with λ=0\lambda=0, implemented through the least squares GPTQ formulation. Then, for each column 𝐰\mathbf{w} of WW, the corresponding outputs 𝐪\mathbf{q} and 𝐫\mathbf{r} satisfy

‖X​𝐰−X⁡(𝐪+L​𝐫)‖22≤δ24​‖X−Xr‖F2.\|X\mathbf{w}-X(\mathbf{q}+L\mathbf{r})\|_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{\delta^{2}}{4}\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}.
Proof.

By Lemma 4.2, applied to the augmented matrix 𝕏=[X​X^]\mathbb{X}=[X\ \widehat{X}], we have

‖X​𝐰−X⁡(𝐪+L​𝐫)‖22\displaystyle\|X\mathbf{w}-X(\mathbf{q}+L\mathbf{r})\|_{2}^{2} =‖𝕏​[𝐰𝟎]−𝕏​[𝐪𝐫]‖22\displaystyle=\left\|\mathbb{X}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{w}\\ \mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix}-\mathbb{X}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{q}\\ \mathbf{r}\end{bmatrix}\right\|_{2}^{2}
=∑j=1N|wj(j−1)−qj|2​‖P𝕏≥j+1⟂​Xj‖22\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{N}|w^{(j-1)}_{j}-q_{j}|^{2}\|P_{\mathbb{X}_{\geq j+1}^{\perp}}X_{j}\|_{2}^{2}
≤δ24​∑j=1N‖P𝕏≥j+1⟂​Xj‖22.\displaystyle\leq\frac{\delta^{2}}{4}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\|P_{\mathbb{X}_{\geq j+1}^{\perp}}X_{j}\|_{2}^{2}.

For each j≤Nj\leq N, the columns of X^\widehat{X} are contained in 𝕏≥j+1\mathbb{X}_{\geq j+1}. Hence projection onto col⁡(𝕏≥j+1)⟂\operatorname{col}(\mathbb{X}_{\geq j+1})^{\perp} can only decrease the norm compared with projection onto col⁡(X^)⟂\operatorname{col}(\widehat{X})^{\perp}. Therefore

∑j=1N‖P𝕏≥j+1⟂​Xj‖22≤∑j=1N‖PX^⟂​Xj‖22.\sum_{j=1}^{N}\|P_{\mathbb{X}_{\geq j+1}^{\perp}}X_{j}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{N}\|P_{\widehat{X}^{\perp}}X_{j}\|_{2}^{2}.

Since L=VrL=V_{r}, we have X^=X​L=X​Vr=Ur​Σr\widehat{X}=XL=XV_{r}=U_{r}\Sigma_{r}, and therefore col⁡(X^)=col⁡(Ur)\operatorname{col}(\widehat{X})=\operatorname{col}(U_{r}). It follows that

‖X​𝐰−X⁡(𝐪+L​𝐫)‖22\displaystyle\|X\mathbf{w}-X(\mathbf{q}+L\mathbf{r})\|_{2}^{2} ≤δ24​∑j=1N‖PX^⟂​Xj‖22=δ24​∑j=1N‖PUr⟂​Xj‖22\displaystyle\leq\frac{\delta^{2}}{4}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\|P_{\widehat{X}^{\perp}}X_{j}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{\delta^{2}}{4}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\|P_{U_{r}^{\perp}}X_{j}\|_{2}^{2}
=δ24​‖(I−Ur​Ur⊤)​X‖F2=δ24​‖(I−Ur​Ur⊤)​U​Σ‖F2\displaystyle=\frac{\delta^{2}}{4}\|(I-U_{r}U_{r}^{\top})X\|_{F}^{2}=\frac{\delta^{2}}{4}\|(I-U_{r}U_{r}^{\top})U\Sigma\|_{F}^{2}
=δ24​‖X−Xr‖F2.\displaystyle=\frac{\delta^{2}}{4}\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}.

∎

The preceding channel-wise error bounds immediately imply layer-wise bounds by summing over the columns of WW. We present both the unregularized least squares version and the regularized version, for completeness.

Corollary 4.6.

Assume an infinite alphabet 𝒜=𝒜δ={±k​δ:k∈ℤ}\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}^{\delta}=\{\pm k\delta:k\in\mathbb{Z}\}. If the unregularized version of Algorithm 3 is implemented through the least squares formulation in (8) and (9), then

‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2≤δ2​N′4​‖X−Xr‖F2.\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2}\leq\frac{\delta^{2}N^{\prime}}{4}\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}.
Proof.

Apply Theorem 4.5 to each column of WW and sum the resulting inequalities over all N′N^{\prime} columns. ∎

Corollary 4.7.

Assume an infinite alphabet 𝒜=𝒜δ={±k​δ:k∈ℤ}\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}^{\delta}=\{\pm k\delta:k\in\mathbb{Z}\}. If Algorithm 3 is run with regularization parameter λ>0\lambda>0, then

‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2+λ​‖W−Q‖F2+λ​‖L​R‖F2≤δ2​N′4​(‖X−Xr‖F2+(N+r)​λ).\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda\|W-Q\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda\|LR\|_{F}^{2}\leq\frac{\delta^{2}N^{\prime}}{4}\left(\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}+(N+r)\lambda\right). (10)
Proof.

Apply Theorem 4.3 to each column 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} of WW, with corresponding outputs 𝐪i\mathbf{q}_{i} and 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i}. Summing over i=1,…,N′i=1,\ldots,N^{\prime} gives

‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2+λ​‖W−Q‖F2+λ​‖R‖F2≤δ2​N′4​(‖X−Xr‖F2+(N+r)​λ).\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda\|W-Q\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda\|R\|_{F}^{2}\leq\frac{\delta^{2}N^{\prime}}{4}\left(\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}+(N+r)\lambda\right).

Since L=VrL=V_{r} has orthonormal columns, ‖L​R‖F2=‖R‖F2\|LR\|_{F}^{2}=\|R\|_{F}^{2}. This gives the stated bound. ∎

Remark 4.8 (Comparison with plain GPTQ).

It is useful to compare Equation 10 with the corresponding bound for plain GPTQ. In the notation of this section, Zhang et al. [80, Corollary 3.5] gives

‖X​W−X​Q‖F2+λ​‖W−Q‖F2≤δ2​N′4​(‖X‖F2+N​λ).\|XW-XQ\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda\|W-Q\|_{F}^{2}\leq\frac{\delta^{2}N^{\prime}}{4}\left(\|X\|_{F}^{2}+N\lambda\right). (11)

The main improvement in Equation 10 is that the term ‖X‖F2\|X\|_{F}^{2} is replaced by the residual term ‖X−Xr‖F2\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}. Thus, when the calibration matrix XX admits a good rank rr approximation, the layer-wise reconstruction bound can be substantially smaller than the corresponding GPTQ bound. The price for this improvement is the additional regularization term r​λr\lambda, which is comparatively small when r≪Nr\ll N.

We close this section on error bounds by demonstrating how the infinite alphabet bound in Corollary 4.7 should be interpreted for finite precision quantization.

Remark 4.9 (Finite alphabets and dynamic range).

Choose λ\lambda to be a sufficiently small constant multiple of ‖X−Xr‖F2/(N+r)\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}/(N+r). Then the right hand side of Equation 10 satisfies

δ2​N′4​(‖X−Xr‖F2+(N+r)​λ)≲N′​δ2​‖X−Xr‖F2.\frac{\delta^{2}N^{\prime}}{4}\left(\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}+(N+r)\lambda\right)\lesssim N^{\prime}\delta^{2}\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}.

Since every term on the left hand side of Equation 10 is nonnegative, this gives

‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2≲N′​δ2​‖X−Xr‖F2.\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2}\lesssim N^{\prime}\delta^{2}\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}. (12)

Moreover, after dividing the regularization terms by λ\lambda, we obtain

‖W−Q‖F2≲N​N′​δ2,‖L​R‖F2≲N​N′​δ2,\|W-Q\|_{F}^{2}\lesssim NN^{\prime}\delta^{2},\qquad\|LR\|_{F}^{2}\lesssim NN^{\prime}\delta^{2}, (13)

where we use that r≤Nr\leq N in the intended regime.

Thus Theorem 4.3 and Corollary 4.7 show that, on average, the entries of QQ deviate from the corresponding entries of WW by at most a constant multiple of δ\delta. If, in addition, one has the entrywise control ‖W−Q‖∞≲δ\|W-Q\|_{\infty}\lesssim\delta, as one may expect generically, then a finite alphabet of the form

𝒜bδ={kδ:k=−2b−1,…,2b−1}\mathcal{A}_{b}^{\delta}=\{k\delta:k=-2^{b-1},\ldots,2^{b-1}\}

suffices, provided 2b−1​δ≥‖W‖∞+C​δ2^{b-1}\delta\geq\|W\|_{\infty}+C\delta for a suitable absolute constant CC. The additive C​δC\delta term accounts for the extra dynamic range needed to absorb the adaptive GPTQ updates.

This heuristic can be made rigorous by replacing deterministic rounding with stochastic rounding in Algorithm 3. Define the unbiased stochastic scalar quantizer 𝒬stoc:ℝ→𝒜δ\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{stoc}}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathcal{A}^{\delta} as follows. If z∈[k​δ,(k+1)​δ]z\in[k\delta,(k+1)\delta], then

𝒬stoc​(z):={k​δ,with probability ​p,(k+1)​δ,with probability ​1−p,p=1−zδ+k.\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{stoc}}(z):=\begin{cases}k\delta,&\text{with probability }p,\\ (k+1)\delta,&\text{with probability }1-p,\end{cases}\qquad p=1-\frac{z}{\delta}+k.

Equivalently, k=⌊z/δ⌋k=\lfloor z/\delta\rfloor, and 𝔼​𝒬stoc​(z)=z\mathbb{E}\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{stoc}}(z)=z. With a suitable choice of λ\lambda, the arguments used in, for example, Zhang et al. [80, Theorem 4.6] or Zhang and Saab [81, Lemma 3.1], imply that, with high probability,

‖Q‖∞≤‖W‖∞+K​δ​log⁡(N​N′),\|Q\|_{\infty}\leq\|W\|_{\infty}+K\delta\sqrt{\log(NN^{\prime})},

for a dimension independent constant KK. We do not repeat the proof here. The corresponding version of Corollary 4.7 has the same form, except that the factor δ2/4\delta^{2}/4 on the right hand side is replaced by δ2\delta^{2}.

Now choose δ=c​‖W‖∞/2b−1\delta=c\|W\|_{\infty}/2^{b-1} for some constant c>1c>1. Then

‖Q‖∞≤δ⁡(K​log⁡(N​N′)+2b−1c).\|Q\|_{\infty}\leq\delta\left(K\sqrt{\log(NN^{\prime})}+\frac{2^{b-1}}{c}\right).

Hence ‖Q‖∞≤2b−1​δ\|Q\|_{\infty}\leq 2^{b-1}\delta whenever

K​log⁡(N​N′)≤(1−1c)​2b−1.K\sqrt{\log(NN^{\prime})}\leq\left(1-\frac{1}{c}\right)2^{b-1}.

Thus, for fixed matrix dimensions and sufficiently large bit width bb, the stochastic rounding implementation remains within the finite alphabet with high probability, with grid spacing on the natural scale δ≲‖W‖∞/2b−1\delta\lesssim\|W\|_{\infty}/2^{b-1}.

4.4 Near Optimality of GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA

In this section, we compare the information theoretic lower bound in Corollary 3.9 with the upper bound achieved by GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA in Corollary 4.7. While Corollary 4.7 is stated for an infinite alphabet, the discussions in Remark 4.9 show that the bounds in (12) and (13) continue to hold (with high probability) under the finite alphabet

𝒜bδ={kδ:k=−2b−1,…,2b−1}\mathcal{A}_{b}^{\delta}=\{k\delta:k=-2^{b-1},\ldots,2^{b-1}\}

with δ≲‖W‖∞/2b−1\delta\lesssim\|W\|_{\infty}/2^{b-1} when using the stochastic rounding operator. In the lower bound, we use a slightly different parameterization of the quantization alphabet {−B,…,−1,0,1,…,B}\{-B,\ldots,-1,0,1,\ldots,B\}, up to an adaptive scaling factor. To compare the two bounds, we set B=2b−1B=2^{b-1} throughout this section. Thus both bounds share the same symmetric integer range {−2b−1,…,2b−1}\{-2^{b-1},\ldots,2^{b-1}\} in representing the low-precision component.

We assume that the calibration matrix has an approximate rank-rr structure. This is consistent with empirical observations that activations, and in some settings weights, of pretrained models often exhibit approximate low-rank structure [33, 75, 85, 77]. More precisely, let X∈ℝm×NX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N}, with m>Nm>N, have singular values σ1≥⋯≥σN>0\sigma_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{N}>0. We assume that the tail after the first rr singular values is relatively flat, in the sense that σr+1≤C​σN\sigma_{r+1}\leq C\sigma_{N} for some absolute constant CC, and that this tail is well separated from the leading singular values, so that σr+1≪σr\sigma_{r+1}\ll\sigma_{r}.

Let W∈ℝN×N′W\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}} denote the weight matrix being approximated by a low-precision plus low-rank decomposition. Following the discussion in Remark 3.7, we restrict attention to non-spiky weight matrices, and assume

W∈𝔹flat1:={A∈ℝN×N′:∥A∥F≤1,∥A∥∞≤3N​N′}.W\in\mathbb{B}_{\mathrm{flat}}^{1}:=\left\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}}:\|A\|_{F}\leq 1,\ \|A\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{NN^{\prime}}}\right\}.

4.4.1 Low-rank Corrections at the Quantization Error Scale

We first consider the regime in which the low-rank correction has Frobenius norm on the same scale as the naive quantization error one would obtain if they were only using a round-to-nearest quantization algorithm. Thus we consider ρ≍1/B\rho\asymp 1/B as this is the natural scale suggested by the flatness assumption on WW. Indeed, since ‖W‖∞≤3/N​N′\|W\|_{\infty}\leq\sqrt{3}/\sqrt{NN^{\prime}}, a natural grid spacing is δ≍1/(B​N​N′)\delta\asymp 1/(B\sqrt{NN^{\prime}}). A naive round-to-nearest quantization of WW then has entrywise error at most δ/2\delta/2, and hence Frobenius error ≲1/B\lesssim 1/B. Thus, in this regime, the low-rank component is allowed to compensate for an error of the same order as the initial quantization error.

By Corollary 3.9, there exists a matrix WW satisfying ‖W‖F≤1\|W\|_{F}\leq 1 and ‖W‖∞≤3/N​N′\|W\|_{\infty}\leq\sqrt{3}/\sqrt{NN^{\prime}} such that

infM∈𝕊Br,ρ∩𝔹F2‖X⁡(M−W)‖F2≳(1(2​B+1)JJ−1​(41​π​e6​ρ)1J−1)2​σN2,\inf_{M\in\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho}\cap\mathbb{B}_{F}^{2}}\|X(M-W)\|_{F}^{2}\gtrsim\left(\frac{1}{(2B+1)^{\frac{J}{J-1}}\left(41\sqrt{\frac{\pi e}{6}}\rho\right)^{\frac{1}{J-1}}}\right)^{2}\sigma_{N}^{2},

where J=J⁡(r,N,N′)=N​N′/(r⁡(N+N′+1)+2)∈(1,∞)J=J(r,N,N^{\prime})=NN^{\prime}/(r(N+N^{\prime}+1)+2)\in(1,\infty). Now write ρ=ρ~/B\rho=\tilde{\rho}/B, where ρ~≍1\tilde{\rho}\asymp 1. Since J/(J−1)=1+1/(J−1)J/(J-1)=1+1/(J-1), the denominator above is bounded above by B​C11/(J−1)B\,C_{1}^{1/(J-1)} for a positive constant C1C_{1} depending only on ρ~\tilde{\rho} and absolute numerical constants. Consequently,

infM∈𝕊Br,ρ∩𝔹F2∥X(M−W)∥F2≳C1−2/(J−1)σN2B2.\inf_{M\in\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho}\cap\mathbb{B}_{F}^{2}}\|X(M-W)\|_{F}^{2}\gtrsim C_{1}^{-2/(J-1)}\frac{\sigma_{N}^{2}}{B^{2}}.

In the simplifying case N=N′N=N^{\prime}, one has

1J−1=r⁡(2​N+1)+2N2−r⁡(2​N+1)−2.\frac{1}{J-1}=\frac{r(2N+1)+2}{N^{2}-r(2N+1)-2}.

Thus, when r≪Nr\ll N, the factor C1−2/(J−1)C_{1}^{-2/(J-1)} is close to a constant and has first-order behavior governed by r/Nr/N since C1−2/(J−1)=exp(−2​log⁡C1J−1)≈1−4logC1⋅rNC_{1}^{-2/(J-1)}=\exp\left(-\frac{2\log C_{1}}{J-1}\right)\approx 1-4\log C_{1}\cdot\frac{r}{N} .

We now compare this lower bound with the upper bound achieved by Algorithm 3. Let QQ and L​RLR denote the low-precision and low-rank components returned by GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA using XX as the calibration matrix. By Remark 4.9, we may choose δ≲‖W‖∞/B\delta\lesssim\|W\|_{\infty}/B, and therefore, under the flatness assumption on WW, δ2≲1N​N′​B2.\delta^{2}\lesssim\frac{1}{NN^{\prime}B^{2}}. Moreover, the spectral assumption on XX gives

‖X−Xr‖F2=∑j=r+1Nσj2≤(N−r)​σr+12≲(N−r)​σN2.\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{j=r+1}^{N}\sigma_{j}^{2}\leq(N-r)\sigma_{r+1}^{2}\lesssim(N-r)\sigma_{N}^{2}.

Substituting these estimates into Corollary 4.7 gives

‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2≲N′​δ2​‖X−Xr‖F2≲(1−rN)​σN2B2.\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2}\lesssim N^{\prime}\delta^{2}\|X-X_{r}\|_{F}^{2}\lesssim\left(1-\frac{r}{N}\right)\frac{\sigma_{N}^{2}}{B^{2}}.

The same finite-alphabet discussion also gives ‖L​R‖F2≲N​N′​δ2≲1B2,\|LR\|_{F}^{2}\lesssim NN^{\prime}\delta^{2}\lesssim\frac{1}{B^{2}}, and ‖Q−W‖F2≲N​N′​δ2≲1B2.\|Q-W\|_{F}^{2}\lesssim NN^{\prime}\delta^{2}\lesssim\frac{1}{B^{2}}. Thus ‖L​R‖F≲1/B\|LR\|_{F}\lesssim 1/B, so the low-rank factor satisfies the constraint ‖L​R‖F≤ρ\|LR\|_{F}\leq\rho, provided the implicit constant in ρ≍1/B\rho\asymp 1/B is chosen large enough. Also, since ‖W‖F≤1\|W\|_{F}\leq 1, we have ‖Q‖F−1≲1/B\|Q\|_{F}-1\lesssim 1/B, and hence ‖Q+L​R‖F≤2\|Q+LR\|_{F}\leq 2 for sufficiently large BB. Finally, the finite-alphabet construction ensures that Q/δQ/\delta is integer-valued with entries bounded by BB. Thus the output Q+L​RQ+LR lies in the same constraint class 𝕊Br,ρ∩𝔹F2\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho}\cap\mathbb{B}_{F}^{2} used in the lower bound.

To summarize, in the regime ρ≍1/B\rho\asymp 1/B, the information theoretic lower bound gives

infM∈𝕊Br,ρ∩𝔹F2∥XW−XM∥F2≳C1−2/(J−1)σN2B2≈(1−4logC1⋅rN)σN2B2,\inf_{M\in\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho}\cap\mathbb{B}_{F}^{2}}\|XW-XM\|_{F}^{2}\gtrsim C_{1}^{-2/(J-1)}\frac{\sigma_{N}^{2}}{B^{2}}\approx\left(1-4\log C_{1}\cdot\frac{r}{N}\right)\frac{\sigma_{N}^{2}}{B^{2}},

while GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA achieves

‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2≲(1−rN)​σN2B2.\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2}\lesssim\left(1-\frac{r}{N}\right)\frac{\sigma_{N}^{2}}{B^{2}}.

Thus, for r≪Nr\ll N, the upper bound matches the lower bound in its dependence on BB and σN\sigma_{N}, up to constants.

4.4.2 Larger Low-rank Budgets and the Compression Tradeoff

We now consider the more permissive regime ρ≍1\rho\asymp 1. The purpose of this subsection is to explain what changes when the low rank component is allowed to have substantially larger Frobenius norm than the naive quantization error that would be obtained via round-to-nearest quantization. The main conclusion is that the lower bound is weakened only through a JJ-dependent factor. Making this factor very small requires JJ to be close to 11, which corresponds to using a low rank component with enough parameters to compromise the intended compression.

By Corollary 3.9, there exists a matrix WW satisfying ‖W‖F≤1\|W\|_{F}\leq 1 and ‖W‖∞≤3/N​N′\|W\|_{\infty}\leq\sqrt{3}/\sqrt{NN^{\prime}} such that

infM∈𝕊Br,ρ∩𝔹F2‖X⁡(M−W)‖F2≳σN2(2​B+1)2​JJ−1​(41​π​e6​ρ)2J−1,\inf_{M\in\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho}\cap\mathbb{B}_{F}^{2}}\|X(M-W)\|_{F}^{2}\gtrsim\frac{\sigma_{N}^{2}}{(2B+1)^{\frac{2J}{J-1}}\left(41\sqrt{\frac{\pi e}{6}}\rho\right)^{\frac{2}{J-1}}},

where J=J⁡(r,N,N′)=N​N′/(r⁡(N+N′+1)+2)∈(1,∞)J=J(r,N,N^{\prime})=NN^{\prime}/(r(N+N^{\prime}+1)+2)\in(1,\infty). Since J/(J−1)=1+1/(J−1)J/(J-1)=1+1/(J-1), this can be rewritten, up to absolute constants, as

infM∈𝕊Br,ρ∩𝔹F2‖X⁡(M−W)‖F2≳σN2B2​(C2​B)−2J−1,\inf_{M\in\mathbb{S}_{B}^{r,\rho}\cap\mathbb{B}_{F}^{2}}\|X(M-W)\|_{F}^{2}\gtrsim\frac{\sigma_{N}^{2}}{B^{2}}(C_{2}B)^{-\frac{2}{J-1}},

where C2C_{2} is proportional to ρ\rho, up to absolute numerical constants.

This expression separates the dominant B−2B^{-2} quantization scale from the additional factor (C2B)−2/(J−1)(C_{2}B)^{-2/(J-1)} that reflects the larger low rank magnitude budget. To interpret this factor, suppose for simplicity that N=N′N=N^{\prime}. Then, as we already calculated in the previous subsection, 1J−1=r⁡(2​N+1)+2N2−r⁡(2​N+1)−2.\frac{1}{J-1}=\frac{r(2N+1)+2}{N^{2}-r(2N+1)-2}. When r≪Nr\ll N, this exponent is small, with leading scale 2​r/N2r/N. Hence, up to a first order approximation

(C2​B)−2J−1=exp⁡(−2​log⁡(C2​B)J−1)≈1−4​log⁡(C2​B)​rN.(C_{2}B)^{-\frac{2}{J-1}}=\exp\left(-\frac{2\log(C_{2}B)}{J-1}\right)\approx 1-4\log(C_{2}B)\frac{r}{N}.

Thus, in the small rank regime, increasing the allowed low rank magnitude weakens the lower bound through a relatively mild factor, while the dominant dependence on the alphabet size remains B−2B^{-2}.

On the upper bound side, allowing ρ≍1\rho\asymp 1 only makes the admissible class larger. The output of GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA already satisfies ‖L​R‖F≲1/B\|LR\|_{F}\lesssim 1/B under the finite alphabet scaling discussed in Remark 4.9. Therefore the approximation produced in the previous subsection remains admissible when ρ≍1\rho\asymp 1, and the same upper bound continues to hold:

‖X​W−X⁡(Q+L​R)‖F2≲(1−rN)​σN2B2.\|XW-X(Q+LR)\|_{F}^{2}\lesssim\left(1-\frac{r}{N}\right)\frac{\sigma_{N}^{2}}{B^{2}}.

Consequently, in the regime r≪Nr\ll N, the upper bound still matches the lower bound in its dominant dependence on BB and σN\sigma_{N}, with the gap appearing in the mild factor (C2B)−2/(J−1)(C_{2}B)^{-2/(J-1)}.

Finally, the exact lower bound suggests that one can make the lower bound smaller by making JJ close to 11. This is not a contradiction to the compression interpretation. The parameter JJ is essentially the compression ratio associated with the low rank component, since the low rank factors use roughly 1/J1/J times as many parameters as the original matrix. For example, if the low rank factors are stored in 1616-bit precision and the quantized component QQ uses bb bits per entry, then the average number of bits per original weight is approximately b+16J.b+\frac{16}{J}. For the compressed representation to use fewer than 1616 bits per original weight, one needs b+16J<16,b+\frac{16}{J}<16, or equivalently b​JJ−1<16.b\frac{J}{J-1}<16. Thus, taking JJ too close to 11 may improve the approximation power of the low rank component, but it also destroys the memory savings.

5 Bid-Up: Alternating Refinement of Quantization and Low-Rank Compensation

Let Q(0),L(0),R(0)Q^{(0)},L^{(0)},R^{(0)} denote the output of GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA in Algorithm 3. We now use this output as a principled initialization for further refinement. The idea is that with QQ fixed, we improve the low-rank component using OLrC ((Algorithm 1)). With L,RL,R fixed, we improve the quantized component using a new fixed-grid coordinate update, which we call Bid-Up. Each step is designed so that the layer-wise reconstruction error can decrease, and certainly does not increase.

In more detail, fixing Q(0)Q^{(0)} we update L(0),R(0)L^{(0)},R^{(0)} to L(1),R(1)L^{(1)},R^{(1)} using OLrC in Algorithm 1. Since OLrC solves the optimal rank-rr compensation problem for a fixed quantized matrix, this update can only improve, or leave unchanged, the layer-wise reconstruction error. It is then natural to alternate between improving the low-rank component and improving the quantized component.

A naive update of the quantized component, however, is not guaranteed to improve the same objective. For example, after updating L(t),R(t)L^{(t)},R^{(t)} to L(t+1),R(t+1)L^{(t+1)},R^{(t+1)}, one could try to re-quantize W−L(t+1)​R(t+1)W-L^{(t+1)}R^{(t+1)} from scratch using GPTQ with the same calibration matrix XX. In practice, this may not yield an error decrease. One reason is that re-quantizing from scratch typically recomputes the quantization parameters from the per-channel statistics of the new residual matrix W−L(t+1)​R(t+1)W-L^{(t+1)}R^{(t+1)}. Its dynamic range may be larger than that of the previous residual, and the new quantization grid may not be comparable to the old one. Thus the layer-wise reconstruction objective in Equation 1 is not guaranteed to decrease. This difficulty is consistent with the observation in Saha et al. [55], where many iterations of alternating minimization were used to obtain improvement, while several subsequent methods apply OLrC only once after fixing QQ [16, 79, 45].

Bid-Up addresses this issue by updating QQ while keeping the quantization grid fixed. Given the new low-rank factors L(t+1),R(t+1)L^{(t+1)},R^{(t+1)}, set

W~=W−L(t+1)​R(t+1).\widetilde{W}=W-L^{(t+1)}R^{(t+1)}.

The goal is to replace Q(t)Q^{(t)} by a refined quantized matrix Q(t+1)Q^{(t+1)} satisfying

‖X​W~−X​Q(t+1)‖F2≤‖X​W~−X​Q(t)‖F2.\|X\widetilde{W}-XQ^{(t+1)}\|_{F}^{2}\leq\|X\widetilde{W}-XQ^{(t)}\|_{F}^{2}.

As before, since ‖X​W~−X​Q‖F2=∑j=1N′‖X​W~j−X​Qj‖22,\|X\widetilde{W}-XQ\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{N^{\prime}}\|X\widetilde{W}_{j}-XQ_{j}\|_{2}^{2}, the columns can be processed independently and in parallel.

Fix one column w~\tilde{w} of W~\widetilde{W}, and let q(t)q^{(t)} be the corresponding column of Q(t)Q^{(t)}. Bid-Up updates the entries of qq sequentially. Suppose q1(t+1),…,qi−1(t+1)q_{1}^{(t+1)},\ldots,q_{i-1}^{(t+1)} have already been updated, while qi+1(t),…,qN(t)q_{i+1}^{(t)},\ldots,q_{N}^{(t)} are still kept at their old values. Then the next entry is chosen by

qi(t+1)=arg⁡minp∈𝒜⁡‖X​w~−X≤i−1​q≤i−1(t+1)−Xi​p−X≥i+1​q≥i+1(t)‖22.q_{i}^{(t+1)}=\arg\min_{p\in\mathcal{A}}\left\|X\tilde{w}-X_{\leq i-1}q_{\leq i-1}^{(t+1)}-X_{i}p-X_{\geq i+1}q_{\geq i+1}^{(t)}\right\|_{2}^{2}.

As this is a one-dimensional least squares problem over the fixed alphabet 𝒜\mathcal{A}, it has the closed form

qi(t+1)=𝒬⁡(⟨Xi,X​w~−X≤i−1​q≤i−1(t+1)−X≥i+1​q≥i+1(t)⟩‖Xi‖22).q_{i}^{(t+1)}=\mathcal{Q}\left(\frac{\left\langle X_{i},\,X\tilde{w}-X_{\leq i-1}q_{\leq i-1}^{(t+1)}-X_{\geq i+1}q_{\geq i+1}^{(t)}\right\rangle}{\|X_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}\right).

This update chooses the best value of the iith quantized coordinate, given the current values of all other coordinates. Therefore each coordinate update can only decrease, or leave unchanged, the current reconstruction error. The memory-efficient implementation in Algorithm 4 performs this coordinate update for all columns simultaneously.

The in-place implementation is important. When row ii is updated, rows 1,…,i−11,\ldots,i-1 of QQ already contain their new values, while rows i+1,…,Ni+1,\ldots,N still contain their old values. Thus the matrix formula in Algorithm 4 implements the coordinatewise update above for all columns simultaneously.

Because the quantization grid is fixed during Bid-Up, every coordinate update is an exact minimization over the same finite alphabet. Hence ‖X⁡(W−L(t+1)​R(t+1))−X​Q(t+1)‖F2≤‖X⁡(W−L(t+1)​R(t+1))−X​Q(t)‖F2.\|X(W-L^{(t+1)}R^{(t+1)})-XQ^{(t+1)}\|_{F}^{2}\leq\|X(W-L^{(t+1)}R^{(t+1)})-XQ^{(t)}\|_{F}^{2}. The OLrC step gives the complementary improvement ‖X⁡(W−L(t+1)​R(t+1))−X​Q(t)‖F2≤‖X⁡(W−L(t)​R(t))−X​Q(t)‖F2.\|X(W-L^{(t+1)}R^{(t+1)})-XQ^{(t)}\|_{F}^{2}\leq\|X(W-L^{(t)}R^{(t)})-XQ^{(t)}\|_{F}^{2}. Combining the two inequalities, one full refinement cycle satisfies

‖X⁡(W−L(t+1)​R(t+1))−X​Q(t+1)‖F2≤‖X⁡(W−L(t)​R(t))−X​Q(t)‖F2.\|X(W-L^{(t+1)}R^{(t+1)})-XQ^{(t+1)}\|_{F}^{2}\leq\|X(W-L^{(t)}R^{(t)})-XQ^{(t)}\|_{F}^{2}.

Thus GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA provides a provably controlled initialization through Corollary 4.7, and the subsequent OLrC and Bid-Up steps refine the low-rank and quantized components while ensuring that the layer-wise reconstruction error will decrease until convergence. Bid-Up is also not tied to GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA. It can be used as a fixed-grid quantization refinement step after any PTQ method.

6 Experiments

In this section, we present numerical results to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA (Algorithm 3), and the gains from additional loops of OLrC (Algorithm 1) and Bid-Up (Algorithm 4). All results are based on per-channel weight quantization with the standard asymmetric weight quantizer. Experiments are implemented in PyTorch [54] using a single Nvidia A100 GPU.

We first present numerical results on language models in Table 1 with r=16,32,64r=16,32,64. We experiment with Qwen3 [72] models using WikiText2 datasets [51] for evaluation. We use, without modification, the implementations made publicly available via Huggingface [69]. The Qwen3-1.7B and 0.6B models utilize a standard decoder-only transformer architecture comprising 28 blocks, each containing 7 fundamental linear layers distributed across the grouped-query attention (Q, K, V, O) and SwiGLU-based feed-forward network (Gate, Up, Down) modules. The main difference between the 2 models lies in their embedding dimension, which is 1024 for the 0.6B model, and 2048 for the 1.7B model. We construct our calibration dataset using 128 random sequences of 2048 tokens sampled from the WikiText2 training dataset for all data-driven algorithms. Following Zhang et al. [87], the 128 sequences are sampled once at the beginning and used to generate the input calibration matrix XX (or equivalently its associated Hessian HH) for all the 196 linear layers. We use the entire testing set to evaluate the perplexity. Our 4-bit results use the min-max grid, i.e. β=1\beta=1, and the 3-bit results use a scaled min-max grid with β=0.9\beta=0.9. More implementation details can be found in Appendix C.

Following the discussion in Section 2, we choose GPTQ (Algorithm 2) followed by OLrC to be the baseline method to compare against as this approach is representative of multiple recent works [45, 79, 16, 55]. We include the plain GPTQ results in Table 1. When reproducing GPTQ, we apply standard dampening by replacing the Hessian H=X⊤​XH=X^{\top}X with H+λ​IH+\lambda I, where λ=0.01​mean⁡(diag⁡(H))\lambda=0.01\,\operatorname{mean}(\operatorname{diag}(H)). We follow the original approach of the publicly available code in [35] to obtain the lower-triangular Cholesky factor Ψ\Psi of (H+λ​I)−1(H+\lambda I)^{-1}. To be specific, the original implementation first computes one Cholesky decomposition H+λ​I=Φ​Φ⊤H+\lambda I=\Phi\Phi^{\top}, then applies a Cholesky inverse routine to recover (H+λ​I)−1(H+\lambda I)^{-1} from Φ\Phi, and finally computes a second Cholesky factorization (H+λ​I)−1=Ψ​Ψ⊤(H+\lambda I)^{-1}=\Psi\Psi^{\top} to get Ψ\Psi. This approach avoids explicitly forming the inverse through general-purpose matrix inversion routines and instead exploits the positive definiteness of H+λ​IH+\lambda I. In particular, Cholesky-based inversion inherits the numerical advantages of triangular solvers and reduces error amplification compared with explicit general-purpose matrix inversion. GPTQ* denotes our modified (more robust) implementation of GPTQ using the eigen-decomposition plus QR decomposition approach in Algorithm 3 to compute the Cholesky factor, as discussed in more details in Appendix C. We can observe that our robust implementation of GPTQ noticeably improves the results for GPTQ for both model sizes under 3-bit and 4-bit quantization.

In the 3-bit experiments, the row labeled “With 11 refinement loop” corresponds to applying one additional OLrC update followed by one Bid-Up update after GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA. The results show that this refinement step consistently improves performance across the tested settings, despite the fact that GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA already substantially outperforms the GPTQ/GPTQ*+OLrC baselines.

Next, we present ablation results for vision transformers on the ImageNet classification benchmark. We use ILSVRC-2012 [14], a 1000-class dataset with 1.28 million training images and 50 thousand validation images. Images are preprocessed in the standard way: each image is resized to 256×256256\times 256, followed by a normalized 224×224224\times 224 center crop. Both models are loaded from the Hugging Face timm library [68] using the patch16_224 variants.

We evaluate the top-1 accuracy of the original and quantized models on the full validation set. For all data-driven algorithms, we use batches of size 20482048 to generate calibration data. Following Zhang et al. [82], we use a new batch of 2048 images to form the calibration matrix XX for each layer. Within a given layer, the same XX is used for GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA and for all subsequent OLrC and Bid-Up refinement loops.

Table 2 reports results for DeiT-B [62], which has 86 million parameters. The original top-1 accuracy is 81.74%81.74\%. For this model, we use the per-channel scaling parameter β=0.6\beta=0.6. Under 2-bit quantization, the accuracy drops to 74.54%74.54\% with GPTQ and 74.55%74.55\% with GPTQ*. Similarly, Table 3 reports results for DeiT-III-L [63], which has 304 million parameters. The original top-1 accuracy is 84.59%84.59\%. For this model, we use β=0.7\beta=0.7. Under 2-bit quantization, the accuracy drops to 80.73%80.73\% with GPTQ and 80.70%80.70\% with GPTQ*.

For these vision transformer experiments, GPTQ* gives nearly the same results as GPTQ. This is consistent with the empirical observation that the calibration matrices XX arising in vision transformers are much less ill-conditioned than those arising in language models. Better conditioning improves the numerical stability of Cholesky-based quantization algorithms, but it can also leave less room for improvement from the more robust Cholesky computation used in GPTQ*. Nevertheless, Table 2 and Table 3 show that GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA still recovers a substantial portion of the lost accuracy, and that additional OLrC and Bid-Up refinement loops can further improve performance.

The column labeled bL=4,bR=8b_{L}=4,\ b_{R}=8 in both tables reports results in which the low-rank factors are themselves quantized. Specifically, the left factor LL, which serves as the feature extraction factor, is quantized to 4 bits with per-column scaling, while the right factor RR, which serves as the error absorption factor, is quantized to 8 bits with per-row scaling. The corresponding scaling factors can be combined across the rank dimension, so only rr additional full-precision scaling factors need to be stored, which is negligible relative to the model size. In these experiments, L=VrL=V_{r} is quantized by round-to-nearest before forming the augmented Hessian in Algorithm 3. This allows GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA to absorb the rounding error introduced by quantizing LL. The factor RR, on the other hand, is first computed in full precision by Algorithm 3 and then quantized by round-to-nearest. The results show that quantizing the low-rank factors from FP32 to low precision is often essentially lossless, and in several cases even improves accuracy.

7 Conclusions and Future Work

In this paper, we establish, to our knowledge, the first information-theoretic lower bounds on the layer-wise reconstruction error for low-precision quantization with low-rank compensation. We also propose GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA, an efficient training-free algorithm that uses only a small calibration dataset, and that matches these lower bounds in scaling up to constants and mild factors. We also propose Bid-Up, a fixed-grid quantization refinement technique that can be combined with the low-rank compensation method OLrC to further refine both the low-precision and low-rank components produced by GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA. Our numerical results demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA, as well as the additional gains obtained from refinement loops combining OLrC and Bid-Up.

None of the methods proposed in this paper requires training with labeled data. A natural next step is to use the output of GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA, possibly after additional OLrC and Bid-Up refinement loops, as an initialization for fine tuning the low-rank adapters while keeping the quantized weights fixed [18, 16]. We leave this direction to future work in order to preserve the concise and theory-focused scope of the present paper, and also because of our limited computational resources.

The near-optimality of GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA may also inform scaling laws for compressed representations. Existing work has primarily focused on unified scaling laws for sparsity and low-precision quantization [24, 53]. Extending such results to include low-rank representations remains an open problem. In particular, it would be interesting to develop a unified rate-distortion framework, based on effective bit-width, that can characterize representations combining low-precision, low-rank, and sparse components. A complementary direction is to develop improved budget allocation strategies for bit-width and rank across layers [89], rather than using uniform allocations throughout the network, in order to more closely approach the rate-distortion Pareto frontier.

Other possible directions include incorporating preprocessing rotations [1, 6, 47] into GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA, extending the framework to activation quantization [70] and KV cache quantization [46, 66], and exploring the interplay with microscaling under different quantization data types [7, 13, 20].

Appendix A Proofs

A.1 Proof of Theorem 3.1

Proof.

By transposing if necessary, it suffices to consider the case N≥N′N\geq N^{\prime}, since the operator norm is invariant under transposition and the transpose of a rank-one matrix is rank one. If N′=1N^{\prime}=1, the claim is immediate, so we assume N′≥2N^{\prime}\geq 2.

It also suffices to prove the result for δ=1\delta=1. Indeed, let ϵ>0\epsilon>0 be arbitrary. Applying the δ=1\delta=1 case to W/δW/\delta with tolerance ϵ/δ\epsilon/\delta gives Z∈ℤN×N′Z\in\mathbb{Z}^{N\times N^{\prime}} and a rank-one correction a​b⊤ab^{\top} such that ‖Wδ−(Z+a​b⊤)‖op<ϵδ.\left\|\frac{W}{\delta}-(Z+ab^{\top})\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\frac{\epsilon}{\delta}. Multiplying by δ\delta gives ‖W−(δ​Z+(δ​a)​b⊤)‖op<ϵ.\|W-(\delta Z+(\delta a)b^{\top})\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\epsilon. Thus, from now on, assume δ=1\delta=1.

Choose irrational numbers α1,…,αN′−1\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{N^{\prime}-1} such that the set {1,α1,…,αN′−1}\{1,\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{N^{\prime}-1}\} is linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. For example one may pick αi=pi\alpha_{i}=\sqrt{p_{i}} where pip_{i} is the ii-th prime number. For 1≤i≤N′−11\leq i\leq N^{\prime}-1, define ui=ei+αi​eN′∈ℝN′u_{i}=e_{i}+\alpha_{i}e_{N^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}} where eie_{i} denotes the ii-th standard basis vector in ℝN′\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}}. Let U∈ℝN′×N′−1U\in\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}\times N^{\prime}-1} be a matrix whose columns are the vectors uiu_{i}.

We claim that

{U⊤​c|c∈ℤN′}⊆ℝN′−1\{U^{\top}c\ |\ c\in\mathbb{Z}^{N^{\prime}}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}-1}

is dense in ℝN′−1\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}-1}. Indeed, ⟨ui,c⟩=⟨ei,c⟩+αi​⟨eN,c⟩=ci+αi​cN≡αi​cNmodℤ\langle u_{i},c\rangle=\langle e_{i},c\rangle+\alpha_{i}\langle e_{N},c\rangle=c_{i}+\alpha_{i}c_{N}\equiv\alpha_{i}c_{N}\mod\mathbbm{Z}. Since the integers ci,1≤i≤N′−1c_{i},1\leq i\leq N^{\prime}-1 may be chosen freely, it suffices to show that

{cN​(α1αN′−1)modℤ|cN∈ℤ}⊆𝕋N′−1\left\{c_{N}\begin{pmatrix}\alpha_{1}\\ \vdots\\ \alpha_{N^{\prime}-1}\end{pmatrix}\mod\mathbb{Z}\ |\ c_{N}\in\mathbb{Z}\right\}\subseteq\mathbb{T}^{N^{\prime}-1}

is dense in the Torus 𝕋N′−1\mathbb{T}^{N^{\prime}-1}. This follows from the (discrete) Kronecker-Weyl equidistribution theorem [2] because 1,α1,…,αN′−11,\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{N^{\prime}-1} are linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Now, take the Q​RQR-decomposition U=V​RU=VR where V∈ℝN′×N′−1V\in\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}\times N^{\prime}-1} has orthonomal columns and RR is invertible. Since U⊤​c=R⊤​V⊤​c,U^{\top}c=R^{\top}V^{\top}c, and R⊤R^{\top} is invertible, the set S:={V⊤​c:c∈ℤN′}S:=\{V^{\top}c:c\in\mathbb{Z}^{N^{\prime}}\} is also dense in ℝN′−1\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}-1}.

We proceed to approximate each row of W​V∈ℝN×N′−1WV\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}-1} by elements of SS. Indeed, since SS is dense, there exists z1,…,zN∈ℤN′z_{1},...,z_{N}\in\mathbb{Z}^{N^{\prime}} such that

Z:=[z1⊤zN⊤]∈ℤN×N′Z:=\begin{bmatrix}z_{1}^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ z_{N}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{Z}^{N\times N^{\prime}}

satisfies ‖Z​V−W​V‖F=‖(Z−W)​V‖F<ϵ.\|ZV-WV\|_{F}=\|(Z-W)V\|_{F}<\epsilon. Let v1,…,vN′−1v_{1},\ldots,v_{N^{\prime}-1} denote the columns of VV. Then it follows that for any v∈span⁡{v1,…,vN′−1}⊆ℝN′v\in\mathrm{span}\{v_{1},...,v_{N^{\prime}-1}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{N^{\prime}} with ‖v‖2=1\|v\|_{2}=1, we have ‖(Q−W)​v‖2<ϵ.\|(Q-W)v\|_{2}<\epsilon.

Finally, we let T=span{v1,…,vN′−1)T=\mathrm{span}\{v_{1},...,v_{N^{\prime}-1}) and denote σi​(Q−W)\sigma_{i}(Q-W) to be the iith largest singular value of Q−WQ-W. By the Courant-Fischer Theorem[34]

σ2​(Q−W)=mindimE=N′−1⁡‖(Q−W)|E‖o​p≤‖(Q−W)|T‖o​p<ϵ.\sigma_{2}(Q-W)=\min_{\dim E=N^{\prime}-1}\|(Q-W)|_{E}\|_{op}\leq\|(Q-W)|_{T}\|_{op}<\epsilon.

Therefore, picking the best rank-one approximation a​b⊤ab^{\top} to W−QW-Q yields

‖W−(Q+a​b⊤)‖o​p<ϵ.\|W-(Q+ab^{\top})\|_{op}<\epsilon.

As ϵ>0\epsilon>0 was arbitrary, the proof is complete. ∎

A.2 Proof of Lemma 3.4

Proof.

It is well known [4] that the set of matrices in ℝN×N′\mathbb{R}^{N\times N^{\prime}} with Frobenius norm 11 and rank at most rr admits an ϵ\epsilon-net in Frobenius norm of cardinality at most (9ϵ)r⁡(N+N′+1).\left(\frac{9}{\epsilon}\right)^{r(N+N^{\prime}+1)}.

To form an ϵ\epsilon-net of the one-dimensional segment [0,ρ][0,\rho], take points in [0,ρ][0,\rho] with spacing at most 2​ϵ2\epsilon. Then every point of [0,ρ][0,\rho] is within distance ϵ\epsilon of one of these points, provided the endpoint gaps are also at most ϵ\epsilon. Hence one may choose such a net with cardinality at most ⌈ρ2​ϵ⌉+1.\left\lceil\frac{\rho}{2\epsilon}\right\rceil+1. In particular, since ϵ≤ρ\epsilon\leq\rho, this cardinality is bounded by 2​ρ/ϵ2\rho/\epsilon as both ⌈ρ2​ϵ⌉\left\lceil\frac{\rho}{2\epsilon}\right\rceil and 11 are bounded by ρ/ϵ\rho/\epsilon.

For any M∈𝕊r,ρM\in\mathbb{S}^{r,\rho}, write M=ρ⋆​M0M=\rho^{\star}M_{0}, where 0≤ρ⋆≤ρ0\leq\rho^{\star}\leq\rho and M0M_{0} has Frobenius norm 11 and rank at most rr, with M0M_{0} chosen arbitrarily if M=0M=0. Set ϵ1=ϵ/(1.1​ρ)\epsilon_{1}=\epsilon/(1.1\rho), and let S1S_{1} be an ϵ1\epsilon_{1}-net for the unit Frobenius norm rank-at-most-rr matrices. Since ϵ≤ρ\epsilon\leq\rho, we have ϵ1<1\epsilon_{1}<1, and

|S1|≤(9.9​ρϵ)r⁡(N+N′+1)≤(10​ρϵ)r⁡(N+N′+1).|S_{1}|\leq\left(\frac{9.9\rho}{\epsilon}\right)^{r(N+N^{\prime}+1)}\leq\left(\frac{10\rho}{\epsilon}\right)^{r(N+N^{\prime}+1)}.

Let S2S_{2} be an ϵ2\epsilon_{2}-net for [0,ρ][0,\rho], with ϵ2\epsilon_{2} to be chosen. Taking points with spacing 2​ϵ22\epsilon_{2} gives

|S2|≤⌈ρ2​ϵ2⌉+1.|S_{2}|\leq\left\lceil\frac{\rho}{2\epsilon_{2}}\right\rceil+1.

Choose M~0∈S1\widetilde{M}_{0}\in S_{1} and ρ~∈S2\widetilde{\rho}\in S_{2} such that

‖M0−M~0‖F≤ϵ1,|ρ⋆−ρ~|≤ϵ2.\|M_{0}-\widetilde{M}_{0}\|_{F}\leq\epsilon_{1},\qquad|\rho^{\star}-\widetilde{\rho}|\leq\epsilon_{2}.

Thus,

‖ρ⋆​M0−ρ~​M~0‖F≤‖(ρ⋆−ρ~)​M0‖F+‖ρ~​(M0−M~0)‖F≤ϵ2+ρ​ϵ1=ϵ2+ϵ1.1.\|\rho^{\star}M_{0}-\tilde{\rho}\widetilde{M}_{0}\|_{F}\leq\|(\rho^{\star}-\tilde{\rho})M_{0}\|_{F}+\|\tilde{\rho}(M_{0}-\widetilde{M}_{0})\|_{F}\leq\epsilon_{2}+\rho\epsilon_{1}=\epsilon_{2}+\frac{\epsilon}{1.1}.

Choose ϵ2=ϵ−ϵ1.1=ϵ11\epsilon_{2}=\epsilon-\frac{\epsilon}{1.1}=\frac{\epsilon}{11} so the right-hand side above is ϵ\epsilon. Moreover, |S2|≤⌈5.5​ρϵ⌉+1≤5.5​ρϵ+2<5.5​ρϵ+2​ρϵ≤10​ρϵ|S_{2}|\leq\lceil\frac{5.5\rho}{\epsilon}\rceil+1\leq\frac{5.5\rho}{\epsilon}+2<\frac{5.5\rho}{\epsilon}+\frac{2\rho}{\epsilon}\leq\frac{10\rho}{\epsilon}. Appendix B Optimal Low-Rank Compensation via GSVD

This appendix recalls the linear algebra underlying the optimal low-rank compensation step used in Algorithm 1. The main point is that, once the quantized matrix QQ is fixed, the best rank rr correction is a weighted low-rank approximation. This can be expressed either through a generalized singular value decomposition or, more generally, as a special case of Penrose regression.

Consider a matrix A∈ℝm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. Its singular value decomposition is A=U​Σ​V⊤A=U\Sigma V^{\top}, where UU and VV are orthogonal matrices and Σ\Sigma is diagonal, with nonnegative diagonal entries in decreasing order. The columns of UU and VV are the left and right singular directions of AA, while the diagonal entries of Σ\Sigma are the singular values. We will use the SVD through the Eckart-Young theorem [19]. Namely, for any positive integer k≤rank⁡(A)k\leq\operatorname{rank}(A), the best rank kk approximation to AA, in both Frobenius and operator norm, is Ak=∑i=1kσi​ui​vi⊤A_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_{i}u_{i}v_{i}^{\top}, where σi\sigma_{i} are the singular values of AA, and uiu_{i}, viv_{i} are the corresponding left and right singular vectors.

We next recall a generalized singular value decomposition adapted to weighted inner products. Let M1M_{1} and M2M_{2} be positive definite matrices of sizes m×mm\times m and n×nn\times n, respectively. A generalized singular value decomposition of AA with respect to (M1,M2)(M_{1},M_{2}) is a factorization A=U​Σ​V⊤A=U\Sigma V^{\top}, where U⊤​M1​U=IU^{\top}M_{1}U=I, V⊤​M2​V=IV^{\top}M_{2}V=I, and Σ\Sigma is diagonal. Thus UU and VV are orthonormal with respect to the weighted inner products induced by M1M_{1} and M2M_{2}. This decomposition is closely related to constrained principal component analysis and redundancy analysis [57, 58, 59].

The GSVD can be computed from an ordinary SVD. If M11/2​A​M21/2=U~​Σ​V~⊤M_{1}^{1/2}AM_{2}^{1/2}=\widetilde{U}\Sigma\widetilde{V}^{\top} is a standard SVD, then U=M1−1/2U~U=M_{1}^{-1/2}\widetilde{U} and V=M2−1/2V~V=M_{2}^{-1/2}\widetilde{V} give the desired weighted decomposition. We write 𝒯r​(A)\mathcal{T}_{r}(A) for the usual rank rr SVD truncation and 𝒯~r​(A)\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}_{r}(A) for the corresponding rank rr GSVD truncation, with the weighting matrices understood from context. In the case of Algorithm 1, which is also the formulation appearing in [45, 79, 16, 55], the relevant weights are (M1,M2)=(X⊤​X,I)(M_{1},M_{2})=(X^{\top}X,I). More generally, assuming XX has full column rank, the problem minrank⁡(M)≤r⁡‖E−X​M‖F2\min_{\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r}\|E-XM\|_{F}^{2} has solution M⋆=𝒯~r(X†E)=(X⊤X)−1/2𝒯r((X⊤X)1/2X†E)M^{\star}=\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}_{r}(X^{\dagger}E)=(X^{\top}X)^{-1/2}\mathcal{T}_{r}((X^{\top}X)^{1/2}X^{\dagger}E). In the quantization error compensation setting, E=X⁡(W−Q)E=X(W-Q), so X†​E=W−QX^{\dagger}E=W-Q. Thus OLrC computes a weighted rank rr approximation of W−QW-Q, where the weighting is induced by the calibration Hessian X⊤​XX^{\top}X.

This problem can also be viewed as a special case of Penrose regression [61, 58]. The more general Penrose regression problem is

minZ\displaystyle\min_{Z} h⁡(Z):=‖A​Z​B⊤−Y‖F2,\displaystyle h(Z):=\|AZB^{\top}-Y\|_{F}^{2}, (15)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} rank⁡(Z)≤r,\displaystyle\operatorname{rank}(Z)\leq r,

where YY is given and AA and BB are full column rank matrices, so A⊤​AA^{\top}A and B⊤​BB^{\top}B are invertible. Let Z^=A†​Y​(B⊤)†\widehat{Z}=A^{\dagger}Y(B^{\top})^{\dagger} be the unconstrained least squares estimator, and define G=(A⊤​A)1/2​Z^​(B⊤​B)1/2G=(A^{\top}A)^{1/2}\widehat{Z}(B^{\top}B)^{1/2}. The key identity is

h⁡(Z)\displaystyle h(Z) =‖A​Z^​B⊤−Y‖F2+tr⁡(B​(Z^−Z)⊤​A⊤​A​(Z^−Z)​B⊤)\displaystyle=\|A\widehat{Z}B^{\top}-Y\|_{F}^{2}+\operatorname{tr}\left(B(\widehat{Z}-Z)^{\top}A^{\top}A(\widehat{Z}-Z)B^{\top}\right) (16)
=‖G−(A⊤​A)1/2​Z​(B⊤​B)1/2‖F2+tr⁡(Y⊤​Y)−tr⁡(G⊤​G).\displaystyle=\left\|G-(A^{\top}A)^{1/2}Z(B^{\top}B)^{1/2}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\operatorname{tr}(Y^{\top}Y)-\operatorname{tr}(G^{\top}G).

Consequently, minimizing (15) is equivalent to computing a best rank rr approximation of GG. Hence the minimizer is obtained by the rank rr GSVD truncation of Z^\widehat{Z} with respect to (A⊤​A,B⊤​B)(A^{\top}A,B^{\top}B), namely Z⋆=𝒯~r​(Z^)Z^{\star}=\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}_{r}(\widehat{Z}).

This general solution also appears in low-rank compression of neural networks. For example, the Optimal Brain Decomposition method of Li et al. [42] considers minrank⁡(M)≤r⁡‖Lx⊤​(W−M)​Lg‖F2\min_{\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r}\|L_{x}^{\top}(W-M)L_{g}\|_{F}^{2}, where LxL_{x} and LgL_{g} are Cholesky factors of the input Hessian HxH_{x} and output-gradient Hessian HgH_{g}, respectively. The proposed solution (Lx⊤)−1​𝒯r​(Lx⊤​W​Lg)​Lg−1(L_{x}^{\top})^{-1}\mathcal{T}_{r}(L_{x}^{\top}WL_{g})L_{g}^{-1} is precisely a truncated GSVD of WW with respect to (Hx,Hg)(H_{x},H_{g}), where Lx⊤L_{x}^{\top} and LgL_{g} play the roles of Hx1/2H_{x}^{1/2} and Hg1/2H_{g}^{1/2}.

Finally, the truncated SVD and GSVD can often be computed efficiently using randomized numerical linear algebra. Dense SVD or eigendecomposition costs 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}) for an N×NN\times N matrix, which can be expensive when NN is large. In the low-rank regime, randomized Krylov methods such as RBKI [64] can compute truncated approximations using roughly 𝒪⁡(N2​r)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}r) operations for dense matrices, while column Nyström methods such as RPCholesky [9] can have cost on the order of 𝒪⁡(N​r2)\mathcal{O}(Nr^{2}), depending on the access model. Fast least squares solvers tailored to machine learning optimization provide another related approach [49, 50].

Appendix C Implementation Details: Dampening and Stable Triangular Factorization

This section describes some numerical choices used in our implementation. First, we explain how dampening is applied consistently across OLrC and Bid-Up during refinement. Second, we describe a stable way to compute the triangular factor needed by GPTQ and GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA. This second point is important because the augmented Hessian used in GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA is singular before regularization and can remain highly ill-conditioned after standard dampening. The goal of the procedure below is not to change the underlying GPTQ update, but to compute the same inverse-Hessian factor more robustly, so that the regularization parameter λ\lambda can be chosen for the quantization objective rather than for the numerical success of a Cholesky decomposition.

Dampening for OLrC and Bid-Up.

When implementing OLrC (Algorithm 1), we use the same dampened Hessian as in GPTQ. That is, we replace H=X⊤​XH=X^{\top}X by H+λ​IH+\lambda I when computing the matrix square root and inverse square root needed in the GSVD formulation. This improves numerical stability when computing (H+λ​I)1/2(H+\lambda I)^{1/2} and (H+λI)−1/2(H+\lambda I)^{-1/2} by eigen-decomposition. We also remark that computing the full SVD (using torch.svd) before truncation to rank rr is not only computationally unnecessary, but may even fail due to the SVD routine not converging. We thus use torch.svd_lowrank (based on a randomized procedure in [27]) to directly compute the best low rank approximation with a slightly enlarged target rank, say r+10r+10, then truncate to the target rank rr.

Bid-Up (Algorithm 4) only requires the reciprocal of the diagonal entries of the Hessian, and therefore does not have the same numerical stability issue associated with matrix square roots or inverse square roots. Nevertheless, in our refinement loops we also replace HH by H+λ​IH+\lambda I in Bid-Up. The reason is that the OLrC and Bid-Up steps are meant to alternate on the same objective. With QQ fixed, applying dampening in OLrC is equivalent to minimizing the regularized loss ‖X⁡(W−Q−L​R)‖F2+λ​‖W−Q−L​R‖F2\|X(W-Q-LR)\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda\|W-Q-LR\|_{F}^{2} over L​RLR. Applying the same dampening in Bid-Up ensures that the quantized update is also performed with respect to this regularized objective.

Dampening for GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA.

We follow the standard choice of setting λ=0.01​mean⁡(diag⁡(ℍ))\lambda=0.01\,\operatorname{mean}(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbb{H})) to form the dampened augmented Hessian ℍ+λ​I\mathbb{H}+\lambda I for all layers in all language and vision models we tested, with the following exception. We observe that the inputs to the down-projection layer in the third transformer block of the Qwen3-0.6B and 1.7B models exhibit a highly concentrated singular value spectrum, in which a single leading singular value overwhelmingly dominates all remaining singular values and attains a very large magnitude. Only when forming the dampened augmented Hessian for that specific layer in these two models, we choose a slightly bigger λ=0.05​mean⁡(diag⁡(ℍ))\lambda=0.05\,\operatorname{mean}(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbb{H})). In the 3-bit results with 1 refinement loop, we also skip this special layer and only perform the refinement loop for the other 195 linear layers in these two models.

Stable Triangular Factorization.

As discussed in Section 4.2, the augmented Hessian ℍ\mathbb{H} in GPTQ-intrinsic LoRA (Algorithm 3) is more ill-conditioned than the original Hessian HH. In fact, before regularization, ℍ\mathbb{H} is singular because the augmented features include X^=X​L\hat{X}=XL, whose columns lie in the column span of XX. We observe that, with the standard GPTQ choice λ=0.01​mean⁡(diag⁡(ℍ))\lambda=0.01\,\operatorname{mean}(\operatorname{diag}(\mathbb{H})), the original Cholesky-based GPTQ implementation can fail when applied to ℍ+λ​I\mathbb{H}+\lambda I, since this matrix may still be too ill-conditioned. To avoid increasing λ\lambda solely for numerical reasons, we use a more robust procedure for computing the triangular factor required by GPTQ.

Specifically, we first compute an eigen-decomposition ℍ+λ​I=P​S​P⊤\mathbb{H}+\lambda I=PSP^{\top}. Then we form the inverse square root (ℍ+λI)−1/2=PS−1/2P⊤(\mathbb{H}+\lambda I)^{-1/2}=PS^{-1/2}P^{\top}. Next, we compute a QR decomposition (ℍ+λI)−1/2=OG(\mathbb{H}+\lambda I)^{-1/2}=OG, where OO is orthogonal and GG is upper triangular. We then set the lower triangular GPTQ factor to be Ψℍ=G⊤\Psi_{\mathbb{H}}=G^{\top}. Indeed,

ΨℍΨℍ⊤=G⊤G=((ℍ+λI)−1/2)⊤(ℍ+λI)−1/2=(ℍ+λI)−1.\Psi_{\mathbb{H}}\Psi_{\mathbb{H}}^{\top}=G^{\top}G=\bigl((\mathbb{H}+\lambda I)^{-1/2}\bigr)^{\top}(\mathbb{H}+\lambda I)^{-1/2}=(\mathbb{H}+\lambda I)^{-1}.

With the standard QR sign convention in which GG has positive diagonal entries, Ψℍ\Psi_{\mathbb{H}} is the Cholesky factor of (ℍ+λ​I)−1(\mathbb{H}+\lambda I)^{-1}. The key practical point is that this computes the factor needed by GPTQ without applying Cholesky decomposition directly to an ill-conditioned inverse Hessian.

This distinction matters because λ\lambda plays several roles. With an infinite quantization grid, smaller λ\lambda is preferable from the point of view of reconstruction error, provided (H+λ​I)−1(H+\lambda I)^{-1} can be computed stably. With a finite grid, λ\lambda must also be large enough to help keep the adaptive GPTQ updates within a mildly enlarged quantization range. In a Cholesky-based implementation, however, λ\lambda may need to be chosen even larger merely so that the Cholesky decomposition of (H+λ​I)−1(H+\lambda I)^{-1} succeeds. This last requirement is an implementation artifact rather than a feature of the quantization objective.

Thus, for ill-conditioned or low-rank Hessians, directly computing the Cholesky decomposition of (H+λ​I)−1(H+\lambda I)^{-1} can force an unnecessarily large choice of λ\lambda. By computing the triangular factor through eigen-decomposition followed by QR, λ\lambda can instead be tuned according to the quantization tradeoff of balancing reconstruction distortion against the boundedness requirements imposed by the finite grid.
